title: Pakistan vs. Afghanistan: From allies and neighbors to war
body: Pakistan vs. Afghanistan: From allies and neighbors to war Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus Israel Ethiopia German politics Latest audio Latest videos Live TV Advertisement Conflicts Middle East Pakistan vs. Afghanistan: From allies and neighbors to war Kersten Knipp 10/03/2026 October 3, 2026 For years, Pakistan supported the Taliban in Afghanistan. But now Pakistan is bombing its neighbor. How the former allies became adversaries and why negotiations keep failing. https://p.dw.com/p/5Nhw3 Taliban security forces after a Pakistani airstrike in Khost, September 2026 Image: AFP Advertisement On Thursday night, Pakistan attacked targets in Afghanistan . The results of that attack are disputed. The Taliban, the Islamic fundamentalist nationalist movement that controls Afghanistan, says that between nine and 10 civilians were killed, including women and children. But Pakistan claims the strike killed 22 militants and destroyed weapons and ammunition depots. These early October attacks are just the latest escalation in a conflict between the two countries that reignited mid-September, after months of comparative calm. The conflict was sparked again after a series of attacks on Pakistani security forces . On September 18, an attack on a police compound in the northwestern city of Kohat resulted in the d eaths of 31 people and more than 100 injured. A splinter group belonging to the Pakistani Taliban, also known as Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, claimed responsibility for the attack in Kohat, in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, bordering Afghanistan. Pakistan accused Afghanistan of providing the TTP with a safe haven. Afghanistan denies this but clashes at the border and then airstrikes by Pakistan followed. Pakistani security officials inspect a mosque destroyed in an attack in the border town of Kohat, September 2026 Image: Hussain Ali/Anadolu/picture alliance TTP and Taliban: A complex relationship The TTP in Pakistan is not the same as Afghanistan's Taliban. Although it does have close ideological and personnel ties to the Afghan Taliban, it is an independent organization that fights the Pakistani state. Many of its fighters sided with the Taliban during that country's long-running insurgency against international and US troops. This is why, after the Taliban returned to power in 2021, the TTP gained more room and more leverage. This has meant that Afghanistan — a former ally of Pakistan — has increasingly become a threat to its neighbor. Pakistan has asked the Taliban to take action against the TTP, but the close connection between the two make this difficult. "Because of these personal connections and networks, it is extremely difficult for the Afghan Taliban to break away," says Conrad Schetter, director of the Bonn International Center for Conflict Studies, or BICC. How 5 years of Taliban rule have changed Afghanistan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The connections don't mean that the Taliban has any control over the TTP. There are certainly historical connections between the two, but Schetter doesn't believe that equals any sort of strong, direct influence. "The Taliban are simply not prepared to take orders from Islamabad," adds Thomas Ruttig, co-director of the Afghanistan Analysts Network, a think tank working between Kabul and Berlin. "They won't let anyone outside interfere." This means the Pakistani policy of supporting the Taliban in order to gain influence in Afghanistan hasn't worked. Difficult borders There's also another older conflict that has an impact on the current situation. This involves what is known as the Durand Line, drawn in 1893 by a British diplomat and an Afghan emir to mark spheres of influence between British India and Afghanistan. The current border between Afghanistan and Pakistan follows the Durand Line and also divides an area on both sides, homeland to Pashtuns, who make up the largest ethnic group in Afghanistan and second largest in Pakistan. So the border dispute here isn't just about territory, it's also about identity. "Ethnic and nationalist elements play a significant role in the conflict," Schetter tells DW. Many Pashtuns still refuse to accept the border that the Durand Line created. In Pakistan, the country's long-running rivalry with India also plays a part. A friendly Afghanistan would have been advantageous for Pakistan. But India has also strengthened its ties to the Taliban. "While Islamabad once viewed Afghanistan as a source of 'strategic depth' in its rivalry with India, it now increasingly views its north-western neighbor as a liability," an analysis by British think tank Chatham House notes. Pakistan exerts pressure Pakistan still has power over Afghanistan, though. As a landlocked country, Afghanistan relies on trade routes through neighboring countries, and Pakistan in particular. Pakistan can use border closures and trade restrictions to exert pressure even as the Taliban regime is trying to reduce dependence on Pakistan and find new economic and political partners. A Taliban soldier with an anti-aircraft gun on the border with Pakistan in April 2026 Image: AFP Trade and security considerations are now becoming tangled. Pakistan has held talks with the TTP that were mediated by the Taliban and ceasefires were agreed upon . Talks between Pakistan and Afghanistan also took place. But none of the temporary agreements resolved the crucial question of how to prevent attacks on Pakistan from Afghan territory. So in parallel with diplomacy, Pakistan has also been relying on economic and political pressure, for example, by closing borders and restricting trade and by sending Afghan refugees back into Afghanistan. An analysis by the US-based Council on Foreign Relations notes that the Taliban are worried that if they crack down on the TTP too hard, they will drive the group towards another extremist militant group, the Islamic State in Khorasan Province or IS-K. This group opposes the Taliban. The conflict recently escalated to another level. At the end of September, Kabul reported 28 killed and 32 captured fighters who had infiltrated Afghanistan from Nuristan province, Pakistan. The Taliban accused Pakistan of supporting its armed opponents, something Pakistan has denied. "It is known from past decades that Pakistan has regularly supported armed groups on the Afghan side — for example, the Mujahideen during the Soviet occupation and later the Taliban," Ruttig points out. "What's new though is that Pakistan apparently also supports parts of today's armed anti-Taliban opposition." Significant escalation This is turning the dispute over the TTP into a larger conflict in which both sides accuse each other of supporting armed groups from the other's territory. British think tank Chatham House speaks of a significant escalation compared to previous border skirmishes. Worryingly, a conflict over armed groups and border incidents is turning into a direct confrontation between the two nation states. Ruttig believes that it would be possible to contain the spiraling violence if both sides return to negotiations. "If both sides were willing to return to the negotiating table — perhaps with international mediation —there would be ways to contain the conflict and, above all, to protect the civilian population on both sides," he argues. Militants kill dozens of security officers in Pakistan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video In a late September commentary in Pakistani weekly magazine The Friday Times , Pakistani analyst Saqib Ali Khan advocates for several things that could ease the tensions. That includes a reliable channel between Islamabad and Kabul, a separate approach for armed groups and greater involvement of the population along the border. The conflict, he argues, is not merely a dispute between two governments but also a security, border, economic and regional conflict. "Along those lines, there would have to be a shift in perspective on both sides," Schetter concludes. In the long term, greater economic integration is also needed, he adds, so that Pakistan and Afghanistan do not define their relationship solely through security and power issues. This story was originally published in German. body: Fernandes calls Ronaldo and denies Portugal rift ahead of Norway game | Football | Al Jazeera Skip links Skip to Content play Live Sign up Show navigation menu Navigation menu News Show more news sections Africa Asia US & Canada Latin America Europe Asia Pacific Middle East Explained Sport Opinion Video More Show more sections Originals Features Economy Human Rights Climate Crisis Investigations Interactives In Pictures Science & Technology Podcasts Travel Sponsored Content play Live Click here to search search Sign up Sport | Football Fernandes calls Ronaldo and denies Portugal rift ahead of Norway game Cristiano Ronaldo withdrew from the Portugal squad, but Bruno Fernandes says forward remains team’s ‘greatest symbol’. Listen Listen (2 mins) Save Share Fernandes calls Ronaldo and denies Portugal rift ahead of Norway game on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Portugal's Cristiano Ronaldo hands the captain's armband to Bruno Fernandes during the game against Wales on Thursday [Pedro Nunes/Reuters] By AFP Published On 3 Oct 2026 3 Oct 2026 Portugal playmaker Bruno Fernandes said Cristiano Ronaldo remains the country’s greatest footballing icon despite walking out on the squad this week after finding out he would not start a match. The 41-year-old superstar said on Wednesday that he had left the team after coach Jorge Jesus said he would not start against Denmark in the Nations League, a match Portugal won 4-2 without him. Recommended Stories list of 4 items list 1 of 4 ‘Verbal attack’: Israeli reporters interrupt Ireland news conference list 2 of 4 Man City whistleblower Pinto says he ‘received death threats’ over leaks list 3 of 4 FC Barcelona accused of corruption in Negreira case: All you need to know list 4 of 4 Turkish court detains football refereeing chief pending corruption trial end of list The former Real Madrid and Manchester United attacker’s future with the national team, for whom he is the leading goalscorer and most capped player, is in doubt after his walkout. “Regarding Cristiano, I had a conversation with him, and what I told him, and what I repeat here, is this – the most important thing is that, regardless of what happens, Cristiano Ronaldo will never cease to be the greatest symbol of our national team, of our football, and of the country, for what he has done not only in Portugal but throughout the world,” Fernandes told reporters on Saturday. Manchester United midfielder Fernandes called for unity after a tumultuous few days in which Portugal fans’ opinions have been split over Ronaldo’s decision. “He has a reserved place not only among the best of all time, but also in the hearts of all Portuguese people and the most important thing is that we stop dividing things,” said Fernandes. “There are no divisions in the national team, it is one and will remain so, despite any noise that may come from outside… “We are outside of this controversy, but what I ask is that the country does not divide itself, does not make choices, that it respects all sides, but, at the same time, Cris is and will be the biggest icon of our national team, he deserves everyone’s respect, regardless of who likes him more or (who likes him) less.” Advertisement Portugal beat Norway and Denmark away from home without Ronaldo starting and face Norway again on Sunday. Coach Jesus said Ronaldo was a “symbol of Portugal” and said there would be time to speak about him after Sunday’s game in Porto. “I’m going to focus on the team, on the opponent which is Norway, one of the five best teams in Europe. That’s the problem right now,” said the 72-year-old coach. aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo Advertisement About About Show more About Us Code of Ethics Terms and Conditions EU/EEA Regulatory Notice Privacy Policy Cookie Policy Cookie Preferences Accessibility Statement Sitemap Work for us Connect Connect Show more Contact Us User Accounts Help Advertise with us Stay Connected Newsletters Channel Finder TV Schedule Podcasts Submit a Tip Paid Partner Content Our Channels Our Channels Show more Al Jazeera Arabic Al Jazeera English Al Jazeera Investigative Unit Al Jazeera Mubasher Al Jazeera Documentary Al Jazeera Balkans AJ+ Our Network Our Network Show more Al Jazeera Centre for Studies Al Jazeera Media Institute Learn Arabic Al Jazeera Centre for Public Liberties & Human Rights Al Jazeera Forum Al Jazeera Hotel Partners Follow Al Jazeera English: facebook twitter youtube instagram-colored-outline rss bluesky tiktok-colored-outline © 2026 Al Jazeera Media Network

title: England trounce Croatia 7-0 in Nations League as Kane goal run continues
body: England trounce Croatia 7-0 in Nations League as Kane goal run continues | Football | Al Jazeera Skip links Skip to Content play Live Sign up Show navigation menu Navigation menu News Show more news sections Africa Asia US & Canada Latin America Europe Asia Pacific Middle East Explained Sport Opinion Video More Show more sections Originals Features Economy Human Rights Climate Crisis Investigations Interactives In Pictures Science & Technology Podcasts Travel Sponsored Content play Live Click here to search search Sign up Sport | Football England trounce Croatia 7-0 in Nations League as Kane goal run continues Harry Kane scores in sixth successive away game for England as Bukayo Saka also scores twice in Nations League thumping. Listen Listen (4 mins) Save Share England trounce Croatia 7-0 in Nations League as Kane goal run continues on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Harry Kane celebrates scoring England’s fifth goal against Croatia [Carl Recine/Getty Images] By AFP Published On 3 Oct 2026 3 Oct 2026 Harry Kane and Bukayo Saka both struck twice as England ran riot in a 7-0 rout of abject Croatia in the Nations League on Saturday. Thomas Tuchel’s side ripped Croatia to shreds in Rijeka to make it two wins from their first three matches in their Nations League group. Recommended Stories list of 4 items list 1 of 4 No handshakes and a delayed ceremony as India beat Pakistan at Asian Games list 2 of 4 Fury vs Joshua: Why was the fight delayed, and will it be worth the wait? list 3 of 4 How a comedy of errors ‘ruined everything’ for athletes at the Asian Games list 4 of 4 Johannesburg to host India vs Pakistan and final at Cricket World Cup 2027 end of list England captain Kane’s double extended his record goal tally for his country to 89. But the Bayern Munich striker was far from the only standout performer for England. Arsenal winger Saka also bagged a brace as England recorded the biggest win of the Tuchel era. Real Madrid midfielder Jude Bellingham, restored to the starting lineup after Tuesday’s 2-0 win against Czech Republic, was on target to cap a vibrant display featuring three assists. The effervescent Anthony Gordon netted to make it four goals in his last four England matches before Morgan Rogers completed the annihilation. Chasing a top-two finish to secure a spot in the Nations League quarterfinals in March, England conclude the international break, again against Czech Republic, at Wembley on Tuesday. That should be a slightly more raucous occasion than this tie, which was played “behind closed doors “because of crowd trouble involving Croatia fans against France in 2025. Approximately 6,000 local schoolchildren and 100 England supporters were allowed into the Stadion HNK Rijeka, creating a subdued environment in a country known for its hostile atmospheres. England’s players had taken a dip in the nearby Adriatic Sea earlier in the week, prompting Tuchel to warn the relaxed mood in the camp must not put his team into “holiday mode”. Advertisement But with the Adriatic shimmering in the sun just yards from the stadium, it was child’s play for England as they demolished ageing Croatia to disappoint the youthful crowd. Tuchel’s men took just eight minutes to go ahead with an incisive raid that exposed the talent gap between the sides. Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott, making his first start for England, was the catalyst with a composed pass to Bellingham. Bellingham slipped an equally measured ball in behind the flat-footed Croatia defence, and Kane took a deft touch before stroking a clinical finish into the roof of the net from 10 yards (nine metres). England had too much pace and poise for Croatia, and it was no surprise when Bellingham increased their advantage at the end of a flowing, 27-pass move in the 21st minute. Saka’s cross was too high for his teammates, but Gordon adroitly controlled the ball in midair and whipped it back into the six-yard box, where Bellingham stretched to poke into the far corner. Gordon put the result beyond doubt in the 39th minute, diving to meet Jarell Quansah’s pin-point cross with an agile header that flashed past Dominik Livakovic from six yards (5.5 metres). Quansah’s assist was a timely riposte to the critics who said Tuchel was wrong to select him instead of Trent Alexander-Arnold after the Real Madrid right-back made his first England start in nearly two years against Czech Republic. England beat Croatia 4-2 in June in their opening World Cup group game, but this was a far more one-sided encounter. Bellingham was in an irrepressible mood, driving into the Croatia area and baffling Luka Modric with a smooth drag-back before crossing low towards Saka, who slotted home from close range on the stroke of half-time. England showed no mercy after the interval, and Kane netted again in the 53rd minute, sliding in to convert Anderson’s cross with ease. Saka got the sixth from Kane’s pass after another woeful error from hapless Croatia in the 68th minute. Rogers came off the bench to put the seal on England’s swaggering display, rounding Livakovic to net from Bellingham’s 87th-minute pass. aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo Advertisement About About Show more About Us Code of Ethics Terms and Conditions EU/EEA Regulatory Notice Privacy Policy Cookie Policy Cookie Preferences Accessibility Statement Sitemap Work for us Connect Connect Show more Contact Us User Accounts Help Advertise with us Stay Connected Newsletters Channel Finder TV Schedule Podcasts Submit a Tip Paid Partner Content Our Channels Our Channels Show more Al Jazeera Arabic Al Jazeera English Al Jazeera Investigative Unit Al Jazeera Mubasher Al Jazeera Documentary Al Jazeera Balkans AJ+ Our Network Our Network Show more Al Jazeera Centre for Studies Al Jazeera Media Institute Learn Arabic Al Jazeera Centre for Public Liberties & Human Rights Al Jazeera Forum Al Jazeera Hotel Partners Follow Al Jazeera English: facebook twitter youtube instagram-colored-outline rss bluesky tiktok-colored-outline © 2026 Al Jazeera Media Network

title: Portugal vs Norway: UEFA Nations League – Ronaldo latest, Haaland, teams
body: Portugal vs Norway: UEFA Nations League – Ronaldo latest, Haaland, teams | Football | Al Jazeera Skip links Skip to Content play Live Sign up Show navigation menu Navigation menu News Show more news sections Africa Asia US & Canada Latin America Europe Asia Pacific Middle East Explained Sport Opinion Video More Show more sections Originals Features Economy Human Rights Climate Crisis Investigations Interactives In Pictures Science & Technology Podcasts Travel Sponsored Content play Live Click here to search search Sign up EXPLAINER Sport | Football Portugal vs Norway: UEFA Nations League – Ronaldo latest, Haaland, teams Nations League title holders Portugal host Erling Haaland’s Norway, days after Cristiano Ronaldo’s exit from the camp. Listen Listen (6 mins) Save Share Ronaldo-less Portugal host Haaland’s Norway in Nations League on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Portugal are set to play their second 2026-27 Nations League match without Cristiano Ronaldo [Carlos Rodrigues/Getty Images] By Manasi Pathak Published On 3 Oct 2026 3 Oct 2026 Who : Portugal vs Norway What : UEFA Nations League 2026-27 , Group A4 match Where : Estadio do Dragao, Porto, Portugal When : Sunday, October 4, at 8:45pm local time (18:45 GMT) How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up and live updates from 15:45 GMT. For the second time in a week, Portugal and Norway clash in the UEFA Nations League. But this time, things are not quite the same in the Selecao camp. Recommended Stories list of 4 items list 1 of 4 ‘Verbal attack’: Israeli reporters interrupt Ireland news conference list 2 of 4 No handshakes and a delayed ceremony as India beat Pakistan at Asian Games list 3 of 4 Dominican Republic bans Haiti from its stadiums after football fans clash list 4 of 4 Who is Man City whistleblower Rui Pinto and what has become of him? end of list Sunday’s fixture in Porto will see the Nations League title holders play without their talisman, Cristiano Ronaldo, after the 41-year-old abruptly left their camp , raising questions about his international future. Ronaldo’s dramatic exit and apparent rift with new coach Jorge Jesus have dominated headlines worldwide. Portuguese players have largely blocked the outside noise, however, maintaining a perfect record at the tournament where they are chasing a record-extending third crown. Opponents Norway have won just one match, despite boasting a talented side that defied expectations with a historic quarterfinal finish at this year’s FIFA World Cup . However, their striker Erling Haaland – one of Europe’s most lethal players – poses enough danger to put Portugal under pressure ahead of this weekend’s thrilling encounter. What is the UEFA Nations League? The UEFA Nations League was founded in 2018 to reduce the number of meaningless friendlies and give nations competitive matches against top-ranked teams. In this competition, countries from across Europe participate in a league structure which features promotion and relegation. Advertisement What is the latest news on Cristiano Ronaldo? Ronaldo left the squad late on Wednesday, shortly after a news conference in which coach Jesus confirmed the five-time Ballon d’Or winner would be left out of his starting line-up for a second consecutive Nations League game. The 41-year-old’s decision to walk out came as a shock as he had been due to train with his teammates at the Parken Stadium in Copenhagen. Portugal’s leading scorer with 146 goals had already spent the entirety of last weekend’s 2-1 Nations League win in Norway on the bench, having captained the side in the 1-0 home victory over Wales last Thursday. He appeared to indicate that the reasons behind Jesus’s decision ran deeper and hinted at a departure from the national team he has graced for more than two decades. “In due course, I will tell the truth to all the Portuguese people about my reasons for leaving the national team, to which I have always been dedicated,” Ronaldo said in a cryptic Instagram post, announcing his sudden exit from the camp. Spanish sports daily Marca said that Jesus and Portuguese federation president Pedro Proenca followed Ronaldo to Copenhagen airport in an attempt to persuade him to stay with the squad, before the player boarded his private jet. Jesus insisted earlier on Wednesday that there was no rift between them, although the 72-year-old, who was appointed in July, acknowledged that his captain was disappointed to remain on the bench against Norway. How have Portugal and Norway played in the Nations League? Portugal are on top of Group A4 on nine points, with three wins out of three. They started their campaign with a 1-0 home win over Wales, before adding a 2-1 victory over Norway in Oslo. In the last match, they thrashed Denmark 4-2 in Copenhagen. Norway are second-bottom in the group, with only three points. They started their campaign with a 3-2 home win over fellow Scandinavians Denmark but suffered identical 2-1 defeats at home to Portugal and to Wales in Cardiff. When did Portugal and Norway last meet? They met in matchday two of this year’s Nations League, with Portugal beating Norway 2-1 in Oslo. Joao Felix and Goncalo Ramos scored for Portugal, while Haaland struck the consolation goal for Norway. Portugal vs Norway: Head-to-head Matches: 12 Portugal wins: 9 Norway wins: 1 Draws: 2 Portugal vs Norway: Form guide (Last five games, latest results first) Portugal : W-W-W-L-W Norway : L-L-W-L-W Who are the top players to watch? Joao Felix and Goncalo Ramos (Portugal): Al Nassr forward Felix has emerged as the reliable scorer in the Portugal setup, finding the net in each of the three games this term. Meanwhile, Ramos, playing in place of Ronaldo, has made up for CR7’s absence with goals in the last two matches. João Felix of Portugal has scored in every Nations League game this season [File: Diogo Faria Reis/MB Media/Getty Images] Erling Haaland and Oscar Bobb (Norway) : All of Norway’s goals in the ongoing competition have come through Haaland (three) and Bobb (two). While their partnership proved successful in the opening match, their goals were not enough in the following matches, as the Norwegians suffered back-to-back defeats. Norwegians will demand better from Haaland, especially after the Manchester City talisman’s incredible start to the club season that features seven goals in as many games. Advertisement Team news and predicted lineups Portugal Winger Francisco Conceicao is doubtful for the game due to a thigh injury. Probable Portugal XI : Diogo Costa; Joao Cancelo, Ruben Dias, Renato Veiga, Nuno Mendes; Ruben Neves, Vitinha; Pedro Neto, Bruno Fernandes, Rafael Leao; Goncalo Ramos Norway Wing-back Julian Ryerson is doubtful with a muscle injury, while centre-back Torbjorn Heggem is suspended. Probable Norway XI : Orjan Nyland; Julian Ryerson, Kristoffer Ajer, Torbjorn Heggem, David Moller Wolfe; Martin Odegaard, Sander Berge, Patrick Berg; Oscar Bobb, Erling Haaland, Antonio Nusa Norwegians need Erling Haaland to be on the scoresheet if they are to beat Portugal [File: Marius Nordnes / Nordnes Foto/Getty Images] Portugal vs Norway: TV channel, livestreaming Portugal Norway United Kingdom: ITV1 United States: FOX Sports, FuboTV, ViX India: Sony Sports Network Middle East and North Africa: beIN SPORTS South Africa: DStv Stream You can find your regional broadcaster on UEFA’s official broadcaster listing . aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo Advertisement About About Show more About Us Code of Ethics Terms and Conditions EU/EEA Regulatory Notice Privacy Policy Cookie Policy Cookie Preferences Accessibility Statement Sitemap Work for us Connect Connect Show more Contact Us User Accounts Help Advertise with us Stay Connected Newsletters Channel Finder TV Schedule Podcasts Submit a Tip Paid Partner Content Our Channels Our Channels Show more Al Jazeera Arabic Al Jazeera English Al Jazeera Investigative Unit Al Jazeera Mubasher Al Jazeera Documentary Al Jazeera Balkans AJ+ Our Network Our Network Show more Al Jazeera Centre for Studies Al Jazeera Media Institute Learn Arabic Al Jazeera Centre for Public Liberties & Human Rights Al Jazeera Forum Al Jazeera Hotel Partners Follow Al Jazeera English: facebook twitter youtube instagram-colored-outline rss bluesky tiktok-colored-outline © 2026 Al Jazeera Media Network

title: Medical plane with 6 on board missing off Massachusetts coast
body: Debris found from medical plane that went missing off US coast - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat US & Canada Debris found from plane that went missing off US coast Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The search for the plane is being conducted near Nantucket, an island off the coast of the US state of Massachusetts By Sakshi Venkatraman and Toby Mann Published 3 October 2026 Updated 8 hours ago US authorities have found debris from a medical transport aircraft that went missing with six people on board. The Federal Aviation Administration told the BBC it had lost contact with the Gulfstream G-100 plane just after 01:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Saturday, while it was travelling from Bermuda to Boston, Massachusetts. The search for survivors continues off the coast of Nantucket, a Massachusetts island, the US Coast Guard said. Authorities have notified the next of kin of those on the flight, four Canadian nationals and two Bermudian nationals. "Search crews located a debris field confirmed to be from the aircraft off the coast of Nantucket," the US Coast Guard said in an update on Saturday night. It added that ships, helicopters and planes were involved in searches that would through continue the night. The plane departed from Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport at 23:40 local time, according to flight data from FlightAware, and was due to land at Boston's Logan International at 01:30 EDT (05:30 GMT). According to the tail number released by the Coast Guard, the plane belonged to Latitude Air Ambulances, a company that provides international medical flights for patients returning home. Among those on board were two pilots and two medical staff, both Canadian, Clarence Togeretz, director of flight operations at Latitude, told CBC News. The crew flew to Bermuda to collect a patient and their relative, who are not Canadian, Togeretz said. FlightAware's tracker shows the aircraft significantly dropped in altitude before its communications went dark, plummeting from around 7,300m (24,000ft) to 3,300m (11,000ft). Radio transmissions shows trouble with communications between the air traffic controller and the pilot, the Boston Globe reported based on transmissions provided by LiveATC.net. "You're coming in blind? Is that what you said?," the air traffic controller asked. "Are you declaring an emergency, or no?" The pilot's response was inaudible. "You're coming in a little weak so I didn't hear what your response was, if you were declaring an emergency or not," the air traffic controller said, according to the Globe. The air traffic controller later confirmed the pilot had declared an emergency. An area fire dispatcher asked emergency crews just after 01:00 EDT to prepare to meet a plane with an "electrical issue". The dispatcher later said "the aircraft has lost radio and radar". title: Algeria sent fighter jets to Niger to thwart ‘coup attempt’, president says
body: Algeria sent fighter jets to Niger to thwart ‘coup attempt’, president says | Military News | Al Jazeera Skip links Skip to Content play Live Sign up Show navigation menu Navigation menu News Show more news sections Africa Asia US & Canada Latin America Europe Asia Pacific Middle East Explained Sport Opinion Video More Show more sections Originals Features Economy Human Rights Climate Crisis Investigations Interactives In Pictures Science & Technology Podcasts Travel Sponsored Content play Live Click here to search search Sign up News | Military Algeria sent fighter jets to Niger to thwart ‘coup attempt’, president says President Abdelmadjid Tebboune says Algiers deployed warplanes to Niamey in late August following an attack by mutineers. Listen Listen (2 mins) Save Share Algeria sent fighter jets to Niger to thwart ‘coup attempt’, president says on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info President of Algeria Abdelmadjid Tebboune called the mutiny in Niger a 'provocation' [File: Antonio Masiello/Getty Images] By Al Jazeera Staff Published On 3 Oct 2026 3 Oct 2026 Algeria’s President Abdelmadjid Tebboune has said that his country sent fighter jets to Niger in late August to help thwart a “ coup attempt ” that shook the capital, Niamey. The confirmation came in excerpts from Tebboune’s interview with local media outlets that was broadcast on Saturday ahead of its full release. Recommended Stories list of 3 items list 1 of 3 Niger military accuses France of orchestrating failed coup: What to know list 2 of 3 Niger military government reshuffles army command weeks after deadly mutiny list 3 of 3 Niger mutiny exposes growing reliance on Russia end of list Tebboune said that the warplanes were sent because some parties had “gone too far”. He added that Niger’s Prime Minister, Ali Mahaman Lamine Zeine, had been visiting Algeria and returned home at night just before the mutiny. “For obvious reasons, this is a provocation against us … and I too will send planes and we’ll meet head-on,” Tebboune said. He did not specify who he meant when he said some had gone too far, or whether he was referring to internal or external actors. Sustained gunfire and explosions were heard in Niamey overnight on August 28 into August 29. A military base at Diori Hamani International Airport was first targeted by renegade soldiers, followed by attacks on the state broadcaster and presidential palace. A military armoured vehicle on the street in Niamey following the attack by mutineers on the airport and presidency on August 30, 2026 [File: Reuters] Niger’s Minister of Defence, General Salifou Modi, announced at the time that a group of military personnel attempted to detain a number of their colleagues at Air Base 101, and opened fire on strategic locations in the capital. Security forces had intervened and managed to contain the situation, gradually regaining control over the targeted locations, he added. Advertisement On August 30 , the Algerian Ministry of Defence said it had sent four fighter jets to Niger following unrest. It said two patrols of four Sukhoi Su-30 aircraft had landed at Niamey airport, accompanied by an air-to-air refuelling plane. The warplanes were deployed at the request of Nigerien authorities on “a mission to support the Nigerien army in confronting an attempt to destabilise the brotherly state of Niger,”  the ministry added then. Niger’s military government last month accused France of orchestrating the failed mutiny, but France denied any involvement in the events in its former colony. Algeria and Niger share close security and military ties, as well as a long land border, with Algeria viewing the stability of the Sahel region as an essential component of its national security. body: Tennessee prison chief to resign after Christa Pike's failed execution - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat US & Canada Tennessee prison chief to resign after Christa Pike's failed execution Image source, Tennessee Department of Corrections By Sakshi Venkatraman Published 3 October 2026 The head of prisons in the US state of Tennessee is resigning after the failed execution of death row inmate Christa Pike on Wednesday. Governor Bill Lee announced the change on Saturday, sharing the news in a joint statement with Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada. Strada said that his stepping down is "in the best interests" of the state, and called the ongoing investigation into the incident "entirely appropriate and necessary". Pike, who was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer, survived two injections and is now in critical condition at a Tennessee hospital as her lawyers seek to commute her sentence. "Commissioner Strada has served with integrity, and I appreciate his willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment," Lee said. Lee has ordered an independent review into Pike's attempted execution and he halted all executions in the state for the year. Attorneys for Pike called the resignation "justified" but said "it does nothing to help Christa now". "What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person," Pike's legal team wrote in a statement. "We hope the Governor's call for a full, independent review will expose the profound problems within Tennessee's entire death penalty system." Pike is being treated at a hospital in Nashville, Tennessee, where doctors are attempting to clear the drugs used during the execution from her body, according to legal filings. She was injected with two lethal doses of pentobarbital on Wednesday but remained alive. She was then sent to hospital in an ambulance. While receiving the two doses, "she could be heard crying, whimpering, and breathing loudly throughout the procedure", her lawyers said. As of Thursday night, she was unconscious, intubated and on a ventilator. The state's Department of Correction has defended the method it used, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out". Authorities have not yet said whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have also not offered an explanation for what went wrong. Her lawyers filed an emergency motion on Friday to preserve "any and all evidence" related to her failed execution. Pike's attorneys previously warned that her medical history and anatomy - including thrombocytosis (a blood-clotting condition) and small veins - meant there was a risk she would experience "unnecessary" pain and suffering during a lethal injection. The attempted execution went ahead after multiple failed, last-minute legal challenges by Pike's lawyers. The US Supreme Court rejected two separate efforts to stop the lethal injection. Tennessee's governor also denied a clemency request from Pike, the only woman on the state's death row. Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer in 1995. She was sentenced to death the following year after a media frenzy around the killing in Knoxville, Tennessee. title: Israeli reporter’s ‘verbal attack’ ends Ireland football news conference
body: Israel-Ireland football news conference ended by reporter’s ‘verbal attack’ | Football | Al Jazeera Skip links Skip to Content play Live Sign up Show navigation menu Navigation menu News Show more news sections Africa Asia US & Canada Latin America Europe Asia Pacific Middle East Explained Sport Opinion Video More Show more sections Originals Features Economy Human Rights Climate Crisis Investigations Interactives In Pictures Science & Technology Podcasts Travel Sponsored Content play Live Click here to search search Sign up Navigation menu caret-left Israel-Palestine conflict Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons ‘This is an apartheid regime’ Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? History of flotilla campaigns caret-right Sport | Football Israel-Ireland football news conference ended by reporter’s ‘verbal attack’ Israeli journalists asked coach Hallgrimsson about the Flydubai attack and alleged racist abuse by Ireland’s players. Listen Listen (4 mins) Save Share ‘Verbal attack’: Israeli reporters interrupt Ireland news conference on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Republic of Ireland communications manager Kieran Crowley signals an end the media conference alongside head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson at the TSC Arena in Baka Topola, Serbia on Saturday [Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile via Getty Images] By Hafsa Adil Published On 3 Oct 2026 3 Oct 2026 Members of an Israeli media contingent heckled Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson’s news conference prior to the UEFA Nations League football match, causing it to end abruptly amid growing political tensions and protests against the fixture. During the media event on Saturday, an Israeli journalist asked Hallgrimsson about his views on an incident onboard a Flydubai flight to Israel earlier this week. Recommended Stories list of 4 items list 1 of 4 FC Barcelona accused of corruption in Negreira case: All you need to know list 2 of 4 Man City whistleblower Pinto says he ‘received death threats’ over leaks list 3 of 4 Turkish court detains football refereeing chief pending corruption trial list 4 of 4 Manchester City appeal Premier League financial breach ruling end of list According to the prosecutor general of the United Arab Emirates, the Flydubai co-pilot “attempted to carry out a terrorist act”, using an axe against the pilot to take over the aircraft’s controls. The plane carrying 174 passengers was on its way from the Dubai in the UAE to Tel Aviv in Israel on Wednesday when the copilot wounded Indian pilot Smit Machchhar, who opened the cockpit door to seek help. The aircraft briefly plunged about 17,000 feet (5,180 metres) before it was brought back under control. The attacker was not officially identified, but media reports quoting unnamed sources said he was an Omani national, Hamam al-Hammami. “What do you say about the people that you support? Their ideology is based on murder,” the journalist asked, purportedly hinting at Ireland’s stance on Palestine and attempting to link it to the aviation incident. Before the Irish team’s coach could answer, the Football Association of Ireland’s communications manager Kieran Crowley stepped in and asked the journalist to refrain from asking questions not linked to the match. The journalist persisted, carrying on with her question before Crowley stopped her again. Advertisement “We respected your questions at the last press conference, but we are doing football questions today,” he said, referring to Israeli journalists’ pointed questions about the calls to boycott the first leg of the European match. Icelandic coach Hallgrimsson later termed the incident a “verbal attack”. ‘You’ve just broadcast a lie’ The first leg of the fixture was played on September 27 and the FAI faced strong calls for a boycott from the Irish public and former players . The match went ahead and Ireland beat Israel 3-0 amid a tense atmosphere on the pitch . Following the match, Israeli supporters were accused of directing racist chants towards Ireland player Adam Idah and were filmed raising military slogans, but evaded disciplinary action from the competition’s organisers. However, another Israeli journalist turned the incident on its head during Saturday’s news conference and accused the Irish team of calling Israel’s players “monkeys” during the match. FAI’s Crowley was quick to shut out the accusation and ended the media event. “That’s a lie. You’ve just broadcast a lie,” Crowley said before getting up to walk away. According to Irish media reports, the FAI is continuing to investigate allegations that Irish players Adam Idah and James Abankwah were racially abused by Israeli fans. An Israeli supporter also led chants about his country’s military from the stands as he attempted to brush aside the team’s drubbing on the football pitch. The day before the first leg, goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu publicly withdrew , saying he felt “it would be wrong to participate in the upcoming fixtures against Israel”. The second leg will be played at the TSC Arena in Backa Topola in Serbia on Sunday. Ireland’s Hallgrimsson termed it “a game with a lot of emotions attached to it”. He said the team was focused on winning the second leg as well. “There’s been a lot of emotions from the people in Ireland about this and obviously that affects the players as well. title: Russia hits second major bridge in Ukraine's capital Kyiv
body: Russia hits second major bridge in Ukraine's capital Kyiv - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East Russia hits second major bridge in Ukraine's capital Kyiv Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Technicians are repairing overhead trolleybus power lines on Kyiv's Pivnichnyi (Northern) Bridge By Ella Kipling and Dan Johnson , Ukraine correspondent in Kyiv Published 3 October 2026 A Russian strike has hit a second major bridge in Kyiv, Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko has said, as Moscow ramps up attacks on critical infrastructure in Ukraine's capital. The attack on Saturday morning injured two people, and damaged the road surface and overhead trolleybus wires on the Pivnichnyi (Northern) Bridge, Klitschko said, causing traffic jams. It comes after the Pivdennyi (Southern) Bridge was hit multiple times by Russian drones this week, with Klitschko warning that "the enemy is tearing Kyiv apart" . Russia said its drones had hit the two bridges used to transfer Ukrainian troops and military cargo. Moscow again urged foreign citizens, including diplomats, to leave Kyiv. The two Kyiv bridges across the Dnipro River link the western and eastern parts of the capital and had not been hit before Thursday. The Russian strikes have severed road, rail and trolleybus links across the wide river. The ongoing drone threat means restrictions on other routes, bringing traffic jams to the city's roads for a second day - though Friday's gridlock has not been repeated to the same level. Many of the city's residents - which number about three million - rely on the metro to travel across the city every day . The fear is this new Russian tactic will result in sustained attacks which could effectively cut the city in two. Image source, Reuters Image caption, In Friday's attack, a Russian drone hit cables of Kyiv's Pivdennyi bridge Writing on Telegram on Saturday morning, Klitschko said "emergency services are on their way" after the Pivnichnyi Bridge was hit. "Traffic on the bridge from the left to the right bank is currently blocked," he added. Earlier attacks on the Pivdennyi Bridge prompted Kyiv's defence council to hold a crisis meeting on Friday. Klitschko warned afterwards that the city was now in a "very dramatic situation" as Moscow was battering its "critical infrastructure, logistics, housing" and other key facilities. Experts say Russian drones are unlikely to bring down the bridges - but repeated attacks will force their closure and risk weakening their structure, making them unusable. More powerful weapons could collapse the bridges, some of which are reported to be in poor condition after years carrying heavier traffic than they were designed for. It was reported that Ukrainian lawmakers discussed the state of Kyiv's bridges in a recent meeting, setting out contingency plans to use ferries or temporary pontoon bridges to keep the city connected in the event of any bridges being destroyed. Russian President Vladimir Putin has said Russia is acting in response to Ukraine's strikes on Russian energy facilities, despite the fact that it was Moscow that had first launched such attacks. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Russia's drone strikes on the Pivdennyi Bridge caused huge traffic jams across Kyiv on Friday After the Pivdennyi Bridge was attacked, passengers described how dust from a blast wave entered their carriage through the ventilation system. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Putin had decided that there were "no rules now" when attacking Ukraine. In an interview with the Financial Times, he said: "The Russians have failed to occupy us. So now they are carrying out massive attacks and mass killings." He added: "They want to destroy our bridges... our data centres, the internet, mobile networks, hospitals, kindergartens, schools, universities - everything. They want people to flee their cities." Putin on Thursday insisted that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian economic targets were a direct response to Ukraine's strikes on Russia's oil refineries and its ships in the Black Sea. "Now from every direction we're receiving calls 'let's stop'. But they started it," Putin said after a wide-ranging speech at the Valdai foreign policy forum. The Kremlin leader admitted Kyiv had "got some results" from its refinery attacks and Russia had lost about 1% of its GDP. Ukraine maintains it began attacking Russian oil infrastructure because it helps the Kremlin finance the war. Russia has targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, ramping up attacks every winter since Putin launched a full-scale invasion in February 2022. In other developments on Saturday: A sailor on a Liberia-flagged civilian ship was killed and another three crew members injured in a Russian attack on Ukraine's Black Sea port in the Odesa region, the Ukrainian port authorities said At least 12 people were injured in overnight Russian strikes on Ukraine's Dnipropetrovsk, Kharkiv and Kyiv regions, local officials said Two people were killed and three injured in a Ukrainian drone attack in the country's eastern Luhansk region occupied by Russia, the Moscow-installed regional head said Moldova, Ukraine's south-western neighbour, summoned the Russian ambassador after saying that five Russian drones and missiles had crossed its border and exploded near "several localities in four districts". title: UK remands 2 Iranians over alleged antisemitic terror plot
body: UK remands 2 Iranians over alleged antisemitic terror plot Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus Israel Ethiopia German politics Latest audio Latest videos Live TV Advertisement Crime United Kingdom UK remands 2 Iranians over alleged antisemitic terror plot Nik Martin with AFP, AP, dpa, Reuters 10/03/2026 October 3, 2026 The pair were arrested on the eve of Yom Kippur and later charged with plotting to attack Jewish targets in Manchester. https://p.dw.com/p/5NhxA Police forces across the UK have stepped up patrols outside synagogues [FILE: October 2, 2025] Image: Andrew Matthews/PA Wire/empics/picture alliance Advertisement Two Iranian nationals charged with plotting acts of terrorism against the United Kingdom's Jewish community were remanded in custody by a court in London on Saturday. The pair were detained on September 20, the eve of Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar. The case only came to light on Friday when the two men were charged, just days after another terror plot, which the UK has linked to Iran , was foiled. What do we know about the case? Prosecutor Mark Luckett told Westminster Magistrates' Court that Rahman S., 34, and Salam ‌A., 36, are accused of carrying out "hostile reconnaissance" on Jewish targets in Manchester, northern England. He said the two men planned to use a "homemade explosive device" and had allegedly been in contact with a third party, an Iranian national, most likely operating from within Iran. The contact is alleged to have given the pair instructions on how ‌to put together a homemade device from chlorine and brake fluid, the court heard. Luckett said the two suspects had used online resources, including images, plans and maps, to identify and research potential attack sites. He told the court that the targets included the Manchester Jewish Museum and the Heaton Park synagogue, where two Jewish worshippers were killed in a knife attack a year ago on Friday. The two Iranian suspects had arrived in Britain in small boats that crossed the English Channel from mainland Europe, Luckett added. One had been granted asylum, while the other's application is still pending, the court heard. The pair did not enter a plea and were remanded in custody until their next hearing at London's Old Bailey on October 23. Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator of counterterror policing, said the plot was believed to be isolated and there was no ongoing public threat. Heaton Park synagogue was the scene of a deadly attack in October 2025 [FILE: October 2, 2025] Image: Ian Hodgson/AP Photo/picture alliance Police find no link to RAF Fairford plot Evans also said the Manchester plot was "not connected in any way" to the suspected terror plot at RAF Fairford last weekend, which Prime Minister Andy Burnham said showed "strong indications" of Iranian involvement. Also on Saturday, police said a dual British-Iranian national, arrested on Thursday in connection with the RAF Fairford plot, was released on police bail. The 25-year-old was the sixth person arrested and then bailed as the investigation continues . Police said the five other men held are all British nationals in their 20s and from London. UK releases air base plot suspects To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Police uncovered the RAF Fairford plot when a farmer spotted suspicious white vans near the base early on Sunday morning and called the authorities. Officers found petrol inside the vans, but no explosives. UK media reported this week that one of the suspects dialled the police about an hour earlier, though that has not been confirmed. Tehran has rejected as baseless accusations of targeting RAF Fairford, which lies 90 miles (145 kilometers) west of London and has been used by US bombers to strike Iran. The UK remains on high alert for potential threats from Russia and Iran. Iran has previously used proxies to commit crimes on British soil, including repeated attacks and plots against Jewish targets, as well as against dissidents. Antisemitic attacks more broadly have risen sharply since Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023. title: What to know about Brazil’s 2026 presidential election
body: What to know about Brazil’s 2026 presidential election | Elections News | Al Jazeera Skip links Skip to Content play Live Sign up Show navigation menu Navigation menu News Show more news sections Africa Asia US & Canada Latin America Europe Asia Pacific Middle East Explained Sport Opinion Video More Show more sections Originals Features Economy Human Rights Climate Crisis Investigations Interactives In Pictures Science & Technology Podcasts Travel Sponsored Content play Live Click here to search search Sign up EXPLAINER News | Elections What to know about Brazil’s 2026 presidential election Polls show tight race between incumbent Lula and right-wing rival Flavio Bolsonaro amid concerns about crime and economy. Listen Listen (9 mins) Save Share What to know about Brazil’s 2026 presidential election on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, left, and presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro in a combination image [File: Adriano Machado and Pilar Olivares/Reuters] By Brian Osgood Published On 3 Oct 2026 3 Oct 2026 For the second election in a row, Brazilian voters face a choice between left-wing candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and a right-wing candidate from the Bolsonaro family . The country’s fractious election is set to take place during a wave of successful far-right candidates across Latin America and a sensitive time in Brazil’s modern political history. Recommended Stories list of 3 items list 1 of 3 Brazil’s Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro still essentially tied in new poll list 2 of 3 Lula warns against foreign interference in Brazil election at UN list 3 of 3 Brazil’s Flavio Bolsonaro to institute debt ceiling if elected president end of list Former right-wing President Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence over his role in a coup plot following his loss to Lula in 2022. The conviction of Jair Bolsonaro and several military officers raised questions about the resilience of Brazilian democracy, revived several decades ago following a period of rule by a United States-backed military dictatorship. An explosive corruption scandal has implicated prominent figures and institutions across the political spectrum, and observers have expressed concern about possible US intervention . Polls suggest Lula, the current president seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, and Bolsonaro’s eldest son, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, are in a virtual tie in a simulated run-off. Who are the candidates, what issues have been front and centre, and what could the election mean for Brazil? Here’s what you need to know about Brazil’s 2026 presidential elections. When is the election? The first round of voting in the Brazilian presidential election will take place on October 4 from 8am to 5pm Brasilia time (11:00 to 20:00 GMT). If no candidate wins the first round outright, the top two candidates will proceed to a run-off vote on October 25. Advertisement Who is Lula? Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva , better known simply as Lula, is the country’s current president and the candidate for the Workers’ Party, or the PT. The 80-year-old has been a central figure in Brazilian politics for decades, serving two four-year presidential terms between 2003 and 2011, and his current term, which began in 2023. His time in office has been defined by an effort to pair political democracy, restored after a US-backed military dictatorship that ruled the country for several decades until the 1980s, with material improvement for the country’s poor through a series of social programmes meant to address inequality. Lula has also sought to forge ties between developing, non-Western countries on the global stage . “He has come to embody the institutionalisation and consolidation of Brazilian democracy since the end of the dictatorship,” Andre Pagliarini, an assistant professor of history and international studies at Louisiana State University and the author of a book on Lula, told Al Jazeera in a phone call. Who is Flavio Bolsonaro? Flavio Bolsonaro has emerged as the heir to his father’s status as leader of Brazil’s political right and Lula’s main challenger in the 2026 election. Bolsonaro is running as the candidate of the right-wing Liberal Party. The 45-year-old is the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. Flavio has pledged a hard stance on crime and insecurity and close collaboration with the administration of US President Donald Trump, which has designated several criminal groups in Brazil as “terrorist organisations”. He has also promised to rein in inflation and government spending, with an adviser stating that he would implement a debt ceiling if elected. Flavio Bolsonaro has also sought to turn his father’s conviction into a story of political persecution, denouncing his trial as illegitimate and seeking his release from prison. “I ask God for the opportunity to walk up the ramp of Planalto Palace next year alongside President Jair Messias Bolsonaro, so that he may place the presidential sash across my chest,” he said at a campaign event in September. “The Bolsonaro family’s pitch is that the institutions that Brazilian democracy has erected since the end of dictatorship are either rotten and unresponsive, and that we need a sharp turn away from this status quo,” said Pagliarini. “The stakes of this election are incredibly stark because the candidates stand for such opposing visions about what Brazil’s recent history means,” he added. Advertisement What issues have defined the race? As with many recent elections across the region, crime, insecurity and cost of living issues have dominated the Brazilian election. Corruption and concerns about US intervention in the country’s domestic affairs have also loomed over the campaign. A Quaest survey from September 7 found that 31 percent of respondents cited violence as their biggest concern, followed by 20 percent who said corruption, 19 percent who said the economy, and 12 percent who said health. While Brazil has seen decent economic growth and low unemployment and inflation during Lula’s third term, those mild gains have been paired with explosive levels of household debt and concerns about the rising cost of living. A report from the Center for Economic and Policy Research, a left-leaning US-based think tank focused on economic issues, found that extreme poverty in Brazil fell by about 40 percent between 2022 and 2024, unemployment dropped to historic lows, and the country’s economic growth significantly outpaced that of most of its neighbours. But the analysis also found that households were strained by a sharp uptick in the cost of servicing debt. All in all, analysts say they amount to a view of the economy that is neither catastrophic nor particularly satisfying. Pagliarini says that both candidates have tried to steer the election onto more favourable terrain for their issues of choice, with Lula portraying Flavio Bolsonaro as a willing accomplice in US efforts to undermine Brazilian sovereignty, and Flavio Bolsonaro accusing Lula of being corrupt and weak on crime. What do the polls say? Analysts say that polls reflect the state of Brazilian politics: deeply polarised but unenthusiastic. “The general vibe is that this is a very downbeat campaign,” said Pagliarini. “There’s not a lot of enthusiasm either way, and it’s hard to tell at this stage who that favours.” Most surveys show a close race, with Lula holding a marginal advantage over Flavio Bolsonaro that tightens further in a hypothetical run-off. A Quaest survey from September shows Lula with 37 percent of voter intention against Flavio Bolsonaro’s 33 percent, while an AtlasIntel survey from the same period showed Lula winning 46 percent to Flavio Bolsonaro’s 43 percent. A Datafolha poll found Lula with 40 percent and Flavio Bolsonaro with 36 percent. Polls also show Flavio Bolsonaro favoured over Lula on issues of inflation, combating corruption, and crime and drug trafficking, while Lula is seen more favourably on issues of poverty and inequality, foreign affairs and health. What challenges has each campaign faced? An explosive corruption scandal, focused on disgraced banker Daniel Vorcaro, has raised questions for both campaigns and implicated members of the country’s political and economic elite across the political spectrum. Reports found that Flavio Bolsonaro had solicited substantial funds from Vorcaro, ostensibly to finance a documentary – The Dark Horse (or O Azarao) – about his father. Advertisement Lula’s former finance minister, Guido Mantega, has also said he helped arrange a meeting with Vorcaro, Lula and the head of Brazil’s central bank to discuss banking policy. Lula has said he told Vorcaro there would be no political interference in his bank’s case, only a “technical investigation conducted by the central bank”. The Reuters news agency confirmed the meeting. The scandal has also embroiled the country’s Supreme Court , with Alexandre de Moraes, whose central role in Bolsonaro’s coup trial turned him into a subject of ire for the political right, facing questions about his own links to the banker. De Moraes has in turn accused a justice appointed by Bolsonaro of wrongdoing, with the court considering probes into the conduct of both justices. What are the concerns about US intervention? Concerns that the Trump administration could intervene or seek to influence the outcome on behalf of Bolsonaro have also loomed over the election. The US president has frequently threatened to cut off economic assistance to Latin American countries if his preferred candidate fails to win. Trump had also used sanctions to target members of the Brazilian judiciary involved in the case against the elder Bolsonaro, which he portrayed as a “witch-hunt”. Trump also placed heavy tariffs on Brazil in a bid to have the case thrown out. The country’s government denied visas to two US officials who sought to travel to Brazil, saying they planned to cast doubt on the integrity of Brazilian elections. Lula’s government has warned the US against meddling in the country’s domestic affairs. Trump has himself used false claims of rampant fraud to justify efforts to remain in office despite his election loss in 2020. A group of 31 Democratic US Congress members recently sent a letter to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio criticising “an apparent effort to interfere with, and potentially undermine” Brazilian elections. The Reuters reported that Brazilian intelligence officials also briefed a French and German delegation in September about possible interference in the election by outside powers such as the US and Russia. The officials said that US interference ranged “from lawfare to interference that is openly acknowledged”. aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo Advertisement About About Show more About Us Code of Ethics Terms and Conditions EU/EEA Regulatory Notice Privacy Policy Cookie Policy Cookie Preferences Accessibility Statement Sitemap Work for us Connect Connect Show more Contact Us User Accounts Help Advertise with us Stay Connected Newsletters Channel Finder TV Schedule Podcasts Submit a Tip Paid Partner Content Our Channels Our Channels Show more Al Jazeera Arabic Al Jazeera English Al Jazeera Investigative Unit Al Jazeera Mubasher Al Jazeera Documentary Al Jazeera Balkans AJ+ Our Network Our Network Show more Al Jazeera Centre for Studies Al Jazeera Media Institute Learn Arabic Al Jazeera Centre for Public Liberties & Human Rights Al Jazeera Forum Al Jazeera Hotel Partners Follow Al Jazeera English: facebook twitter youtube instagram-colored-outline rss bluesky tiktok-colored-outline © 2026 Al Jazeera Media Network

Close In Brazil’s upcoming presidential election, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is facing right-wing challenger and ally of Donald Trump, Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. title: 'Anger in the streets': Tens of thousands protest in Spain over housing crisis
body: Protesters across Spain demand action over housing crisis - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East 'Anger in the streets': Tens of thousands protest in Spain over housing crisis Figure caption, Major protest in Spain as millions struggle to find an affordable home By Ella Kipling Published 3 October 2026 Updated 9 hours ago Tens of thousands of people have protested across Spain calling for greater protections for tenants after the government failed to pass emergency housing legislation. About 50 marches took place on Saturday in cities including Madrid, Valencia and Barcelona. "There is a lot of anger in the streets," a spokesperson for the Valencia Tenants' Union said. Clashes have taken place between some protesters and police in the city. The measures put forward by Pedro Sánchez's leftist coalition government on Friday followed public outcry over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home last month after she was unable to afford a sharp rent increase. Her eviction triggered nationwide protests across Spain with protesters demanding lower rents, an end to evictions, and a ban on investment funds - or "vulture funds" as the government has termed them - buying property. Sanchez's defeat in Congress on Friday heightens speculation that he might call an early general election, which was not due until next summer. His coalition government, made up of his ruling Socialist party and junior partner the Sumar alliance, does not command a majority in parliament. Spanish PM Sánchez loses key housing crisis vote after eviction of woman, 87 Published 1 day ago Photographs showed protesters in the east coast city of Valencia clashing with police officers on Saturday near arts centre Palau de les Arts Reina Sofía, which was hosting a real estate summit. Several protesters removed barriers and threw objects at officers, who responded with rubber bullets, Spanish media reported. Public broadcaster RTVE said nine police officers were injured and five people were arrested. Image source, EPA Image caption, Tens of thousands took to the streets of Madrid to protest Image source, EPA/Shuttershock Image caption, Tensions arose between some protesters and police officers in Valencia One of the biggest demonstration happened in the capital, Madrid, where estimates of the number of participants varied widely. The city's Tenants' Union said there were 500,000, while officials put the figure at 70,000. Demonstrators held banners reading "There won't be peace for rentism" and "I study to have a future, not to have a tiny apartment". They shook the keys they were holding and chanted: "We have the keys of all the city". Some had also camped in one of the city's main squares, Puerta del Sol, for days. One protester, David, told RTVE ahead of the protest: "We're not here for pleasure or comfort. We're here out of conviction." Another protester, 26-year-old librarian Marcos Sainz, told AFP news agency that he used to share a two-bedroom flat with friends, paying 900 euros (£766) a month in rent. Today, he said a one-bedroom flat often costs 1,000 euros. Sainz said he would protest against rent rises "until someone dares to regulate it all", or "we'll all have to leave Madrid". Spanish police said they had arrested three members of a far-right group, some of whom had performed Nazi salutes, as they tried to reach demonstrators in the square. On Friday night, Madrid's Tenants' Union said that although the government's proposed measures were insufficient, the rejection of the proposed legislation "exacerbates the housing crisis which is costing the working class their lives". It is calling for a general strike over the housing crisis. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, An encampment has been set up for days by protesters at Puerta del Sol in Madrid Image source, EPA/Shutterstock Image caption, Huge numbers of protesters rallied in Madrid The legislation put forward in Congress on Friday was divided into two decrees. The first included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by  so-called "vulture funds". The second decree included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the Tenants' Union. MPs rejected the first decree by 178 votes to 172 and voted against the second by 184 to 166. Prior to the vote, the conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox had already said they would vote against both initiatives, leaving the minority government depending on the support of smaller nationalist parties in Catalonia and the Basque Country. However, by the eve of the parliamentary session, the centre-right, pro-independence Together for Catalonia (JxCat) had signalled its opposition to both laws, condemning them to failure. Sánchez's ruling coalition hurriedly drew up the decree laws in an effort to defuse the housing protests that were sparked when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted in September. The social backlash led to the company that owns Abascal's flat, Urbagestión, negotiating her return to the flat on a low rent. However, protests have continued. Dramatic eviction of woman aged 87 highlights Spain's housing shortage Published 23 September Evicted Spanish pensioner can move back home, lawyer says Published 5 days ago The Bank of Spain estimates the country is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction. House prices have risen by 12.2% in the past year, according to figures for the second quarter of 2026 from national statistics institute INE. The shortage in rental housing means that costs rose by 8.5% in 2025, according to real estate firm Idealista, with Madrid alone seeing an increase of 9.7% in rents. It said Barcelona and Madrid were Spain's most expensive cities to rent a home, at €23.80 per square metre and €22.70 per square metre respectively.
