title: Bosnia and Herzegovina is still shaped by war, separatism, EU ambitions
body: Bosnia-Herzegovina shaped by war, separatism, EU ambitions Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus Israel Ethiopia German politics Latest audio Latest videos Live TV Advertisement Politics Bosnia and Herzegovina Bosnia-Herzegovina shaped by war, separatism, EU ambitions Zoran Arbutina 10/03/2026 October 3, 2026 Bosnia and Herzegovina is governed by a system established after the Bosnian war — more than 30 years ago. Ethnic divisions, a complex administration and European integration all shape the country's political reality. https://p.dw.com/p/5Nfi1 Sarajevo, host of the 1984 Winter Olympics, was under siege for four years during the Bosnian war in the mid 1990s Image: Gabriele Thielmann/imageBROKER/picture alliance Advertisement To call Bosnia and Herzegovina a complicated country is an understatement. The country in the Balkan Peninsula divides its economic, administrative and political responsibilities between the multiethnic central government, the self-governing neutral Brcko district and two semi-autonomous entities that, for the most part, operate independently — the Muslim-Croat Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Serb-run Republika Srpska . Both semi-autonomous entities are further split into several cantons and communities, home to mostly Bosniaks and Bosnian Croats in the central-western federation and Bosnian Serbs in Republika Srpska, to the north and east. This principle of ethnic nationalism is key to the country's central constitutional and political organization. The Bosnian constitution recognizes Bosniaks, who are predominantly Muslim, the largely Orthodox Bosnian Serbs and primarily Catholic Bosnian Croats as "constituent peoples" with equal rights. Today, the country has a population of around 3.1 million people. Around half are Bosniaks, while 31% are Serb and 15% are Croat. The rest of the inhabitants belong either to one of the 17 officially recognized minorities, like the Roma and Jews , or chose not to identify with any ethnicity at the last official census. Bosnian, Croatian and Serbian are all recognized as official languages. The central government is led by rotating three-way presidency , made up of one representative from each of the three main constituent groups. The upper house of parliament and key government offices are also divided according to this principle. This strict balance between the three groups is always maintained, both politically and socially, often leading to ethnic interests and political gridlock dominating the decision-making process. Dayton Peace Accords brought an end to war This complex, convoluted and oft dysfunctional structure was set up during the 1995 Dayton Peace Accords , and then anchored in the constitution. It was intended to bring an end to the Bosnian war — sparked by the breakup of Yugoslavia in the early 1990s — and legally secure the balance of power between the three feuding ethnic groups. During the war, from 1992 to 1995, the armed forces of the Bosniaks and the Bosnian Croats initially fought each other, before all three groups began to clash. Later, the Bosniaks and the Bosnian Croats joined forces to take on Republika Srpska. Throughout the war, neighboring Serbia and Croatia were actively involved in the fighting. Bosnia-Herzegovina: 30 years after Srebrenica massacre To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The fighting devastated wide swaths of the country, and resulted in countless war crimes — among them the nearly four-year siege of Sarajevo and the Srebrenica genocide , in which thousands of Bosniaks were killed at the hands of Serb forces. By the end of the war, some 100,000 people had been killed. A further 2.2 million were displaced by so-called "ethnic cleansing," forced from their homes by expulsions and violence to flee to other communities or abroad. The fighting only ended after the international community, especially the United States, stepped up its involvement, culminating in the peace deal agreed at a military base near Dayton, Ohio in November 1995. International oversight — essential, or no longer relevant? Although Bosnia and Herzegovina has been recognized on the international stage since the signing of the Dayton agreement, and is also represented at the United Nations, the country itself is still, in effect, only partially independent. The Office of the High Representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina, an international institution responsible for overseeing the civilian aspects of the Dayton agreement, has been in place since a UN Security Council resolution in 1995. The high representative — Christian Schmidt of Germany until this past June, and currently filled by acting head Louis J. Crishock of the US — has sweeping powers. He can dismiss elected officials, pass laws, establish new government agencies and overrule all the country's democratic institutions. The Dayton Peace Agreement 30 years on To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video This authority is often referred to as the Bonn Powers, as they were negotiated during a meeting of the Peace Implementation Council in Bonn, Germany in December 1997. From 2002 to 2011, the high representative also acted as the EU special representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina. In recent years, there's been much discussion over whether the office is still relevant. Supporters have said the high representative remains a necessary guarantor of the country's unity and functionality. But critics have pointed out the negative impact on Bosnia-Herzegovina's democratic culture, turning the country into a de facto protectorate that, to an extent, frees local politicians of responsibility for their actions. Separatist ambitions surface once more The sharpest criticism has come from the Republika Srpska and Milorad Dodik, its most influential leader . Dodik, in office as prime minister and president of the Serb entity until 2025, views the office and the international backing it provides for a unified Bosnia-Herzegovina as an obstacle to his separatist ambitions. With strong support from the Serbian capital, Belgrade, Moscow — and, increasingly, the Trump administration — Dodik has flirted with several different scenarios to split his Republika Srpska from Bosnia-Herzegovina. In his interpretation, and that of Republika Srpska's political elite, Bosnia-Herzegovina is highly centralized and unitary, which undermines the independence and sovereignty of the Bosnian Serbs. Milorad Dodik (right, seen here meeting with Vladimir Putin in April 2025), continues to foster a close relationship with Russia Image: press service of kremlin.ru A similar sentiment prevails among the political representatives of Bosnia's Croats. Although they aren't considering separation, they are trying to squeeze more independence from the central government in Sarajevo — not least with the creation of a third, Croatian, entity. The plan, incidentally, also has the support of the government in neighboring EU member Croatia . EU support aims to 'foster regional integration' A potential path out of the current economic and political paralysis is rapprochement with the European Union — the "European perspective," as it's called in Bosnia-Herzegovina, officially supported by all the relevant political actors. Bosnia-Herzegovina formally submitted its application for EU membership in 2016, and the European Council gave the green light for negotiations to begin in early 2024. But the actual start of membership talks hinges on the prior implementation of numerous reforms, notably in the areas of rule of law, fighting corruption, the prosecution of organized crime and the functionality of state institutions. EU enlargement: Who's slowing? Who's advancing? Who's next? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The EU has been financially supporting Bosnia-Herzegovina since 2007 in the framework of pre-accession assistance, and the country is also expected to benefit from the European Commission's Economic and Investment Plan for the Western Balkans. The plan aims to "foster regional integration" — and as a result, infrastructure funding for the Republika Srpska has been partially suspended due to its ongoing separatist rhetoric and policies. title: Rising energy costs add to cost of living for Northern Ireland's consumers
body: Cost of living: Energy price hikes in Northern Ireland add to mounting financial pressure - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat N. Ireland N. Ireland Politics Rising energy costs add to cost of living for Northern Ireland's consumers Image source, BBC / Ryan McStay By Adam Mandeville and Clodagh Rice , Business correspondent, BBC News NI Published 3 October 2026 Households across Northern Ireland face increasing pressure on the cost of living as energy price hikes have come into effect. Northern Ireland's largest provider of natural gas, SSE Airtricity, increased its prices by almost 19% on Thursday for its 200,000 domestic and small business customers. That means the annual gas bill of a typical household in the greater Belfast and west gas network areas will increase by almost £172. The company said "unprecedented levels of volatility in global energy markets and higher wholesale gas prices" had led to the price rise. Wholesale gas prices in the UK have effectively doubled since the US and Israel began their attack on Iran. Keeping the house warm is particularly important for parents with young children and babies. Lucy Kells is a mum of two in east Belfast on maternity leave. She said she expects the winter months to be difficult because "most people are going to have to have the heating on, especially if you've young kids in the house". "There's no escaping it - everything feels more expensive and it is more expensive." Image caption, Lucy Kells is a mum of two in east Belfast on maternity leave She added that, despite "budgeting proactively" and "being as careful as you can with savings and credit cards", rising bills mean people's financial situations are out of their control. "You have to cut somewhere else and I already feel we are doing that," she said. Image caption, Nuala Hyde said she has noticed more people using her branch's free activities to combat the rising cost of living Lucy is one of the parents who attend a weekly baby class at Woodstock Library in east Belfast. Branch manager Nuala Hyde said she has noticed more people using their free activities to combat the rising cost of living. She said: "As well as families, we have lots of older people coming in now to keep warm." "We have people coming in who will stay all day, use the computer, have a chat and stay until closing time sometimes, so it is quite evident that we are providing an essential service at the minute when people are struggling," she added. Image source, Ryan McStay Image caption, Ryan McStay said he was "shocked" by the energy price increases Ryan McStay is a final year student at St Mary's University College Belfast, where he is studying to become a primary school teacher. He said he and his flatmates were "shocked" when they received a letter explaining their Firmus energy bills would be rising by 12.5%. "It shouldn't be normalised," he told BBC News NI. Ryan said increases like this exacerbate an already serious cost of living crisis for students like him. "The price of everything is rocketing. You're always second guessing and thinking about how much money have I got." The 21-year-old, who is from Newry, said the cost of living in Northern Ireland means he plans to move abroad after university. "I personally believe the best option for me right now would be to leave the country." 'It's getting worse' Image source, Naomi Campbell Image caption, Naomi Campbell is an urgent hospice care nurse for Marie Curie Naomi Campbell is an urgent hospice care nurse for Marie Curie. She provides palliative nursing care to patients in their homes. "Many of them are affected by fuel poverty," Naomi said. "I think it is getting worse. People are struggling more, and the problem is that your energy needs increase hugely when you're dying at home. "Somebody is already struggling with the fact that they're dying. To then know that they can't keep their house warm." Naomi said a number of factors contribute to the increased energy needs, including the need to stay warm, different sleeping patterns, and essential medical devices. She said some patients have turned down services that could help improve their quality of life because they can't pay their electricity bills. Terminal illness adds further costs for patients, such as the cost of transport to and from hospital appointments, Naomi added. "I'm really saddened," she said. "The support is limited, there is very little out there. There is no reduction in costs of their electricity, even though their needs are so much higher and essential for their care." Naomi added that Marie Curie have called for the implementation of a "social tariff" for people with terminal illnesses, to ease their financial burden. "It would make such a huge difference to have that bit of extra money in your last months of life, so you're comfortable and you can spend it with your family," she said. She said some people spend the end of their life working because they "don't have any other access to money". "You end up dying not being able to keep your house warm. That to me is just devastating." Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Households across Northern Ireland will get a one-off £63 reduction in electricity bills from this month It comes as Share Energy announced electricity prices will also rise by 12.6% from today. This will add an extra £129 per year onto the typical household bill of their 41,000 customers. Head of Energy Policy at the Consumer Council Raymond Gormley said: "This increase has been driven by the continued volatility in wholesale energy costs, caused by geopolitics in the Middle East. "I suspect some of the other unregulated suppliers may follow suit and increase their tariffs." Gas prices outside the greater Belfast also rose on Thursday. Firmus energy has announced an 8.98% rise for 77,000 domestic and small business customers in the Ten Towns network area from 1 October. That means a typical annual gas bill will rise by around £87. It comes after an increase of 15.65% in July 2026. What support is available? Households across Northern Ireland will get the one-off £63 reduction in electricity bills from this month. It will be applied automatically without the need for an application. The reduction is the local outworking of two schemes which apply in Great Britain, which has a separately regulated electricity market. The schemes are being funded by the UK government. Bank payment customers will have their bills automatically reduced while pay-as-you-go customers will receive £63 in credit when they top up their meter. The only complication for pay-as-you-go customers is they should not buy more than £112 of credit if they want to get the discount all in one go. That is because meters are set up to take a maximum payment of £175. Top ups over this value means the £63 payment will be split over a subsequent top up. Last month, applications opened for a separate means-tested scheme to provide a £100 voucher to some heating oil users. It is jointly funded by Stormont and the UK government. Two thirds of homes in Northern Ireland use home heating oil, the cost of which has also soared in recent months due to the US conflict with Iran. Data from the NI consumer council suggests 500 litres of home heating oil currently costs around £560, more than twice the price compared to this time last year. title: Australia: Car crashes into rugby fans, 10 injured
body: Australia: Car crashes into rugby fans, 10 injured Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus Israel Ethiopia German politics Latest audio Latest videos Live TV Advertisement Catastrophe Australia Australia: Car crashes into rugby fans, 10 injured Dharvi Vaid Dhulia with AFP, AP, Reuters and DPA 10/03/2026 October 3, 2026 The driver has been identified as an 18-year-old man who is said to have been "revving" when he lost control of his car. https://p.dw.com/p/5NgVn Police said the driver was arrested and taken to the hospital for mandatory testing [Representative image] Image: Hollie Adams/REUTERS Advertisement A car drove into a crowd of rugby league supporters in the eastern Australian city of Newcastle on Saturday after its driver appeared to lose control, leaving at least 10 people injured, authorities said. Several children were reported to be among the wounded. Two of the injured were in a critical condition, including a 5-year-old girl and a 67-year-old man, New South Wales officials said. What do we know about the car crash in Australia? The incident occurred in Newcastle's Wallsend ‌suburb, situated some 110 kilometers (68 miles) north of Sydney. Fans had gathered on the streets to cheer on the Newcastle Knights rugby team who were leaving for the National Rugby League grand final against the Sydney Roosters, slated to be held in ​Sydney on Sunday. Local reports cited the police as identifying the driver as an 18-year-old man, who was arrested and taken to the hospital for mandatory testing. Driver 'lost control' Newcastle Mayor Gavin Morris said in televised remarks that the driver was a rugby fan and that he lost control of his vehicle. "He was revving the car, he was excited, he was a supporter, he was there for the joy of the moment," Morris told Australian broadcaster ABC. "Somehow he lost control of the car ... and he's gone into the crowd." Police said they were probing the incident and initial inquiries indicated it was not terrorism-related. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the incident was "horrible." "Rugby league brings people together, and this should have been a weekend of excitement and pride for Newcastle fans," he said in a statement on X. title: The South African men trying to end violence against women: 'Every man needs to play a part'
body: Ekurhuleni killings: The South African men trying to end violence against women - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East The South African men trying to end violence against women: 'Every man needs to play a part' Image source, Christian Parkinson/ BBC Image caption, Kgomotso Mathekga says a lack of male role models is fuelling violence against women in his neighbourhood By Christian Parkinson Reporting from Johannesburg Published 3 October 2026 "I witness men hitting women all the time," says Kgomotso Mathekga, 30. "Especially when they are both drunk." "I once had an argument with my girlfriend," he admits, "and I grabbed and slapped her." Mathekga is speaking frankly during a gathering of men aimed at helping reduce the high levels of violence against women in South Africa. The meeting is held in a narrow street in a Johannesburg informal settlement known as Organic Market. It is a maze of corrugated metal shacks and unpaved roads, close to Alexandra township. "Now I feel pain," Mathekga continues. "We broke up and I no longer see my child. I feel like I've contributed to the problems in South Africa, instead of being the gentleman that I know I am." At a nearby tavern, a group of men have pulled their chairs into a circle in the dust. At the centre stands Itumeleng Stephen Tamaga, known locally as Bra Steve. He raises his fist. "We are men!" he shouts. The group clap and cheers. Some sip bottled beer. "Listen guys," Bra Steve says. "We must stand together to fight against gender-based violence and femicide." Bra Steve is the local organiser of Father A Nation, a non-profit that works with men and boys to promote positive masculinity and help end violence against women. The group's meeting comes as South Africa grapples with renewed anger over renewed cases of femicide and violence against women. The discovery of the bodies of 12 women over three months, in the city of Ekurhuleni, near Johannesburg has reignited questions about the scale of what many people see as being a crisis of violence against women. Image source, Christian Parkinson/ BBC Image caption, Bra Steve says: "We must restore dignity to the men around here" South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa has acknowledged that his government has not done enough and announced measures he hopes can make women feel safer. The country has one of the highest murder rates in the world, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone. In that period, according to the South African Human Rights Commission, 569 women were killed, an average of six a day, and 1,052 others survived attempted murder. A report in 2022 by the Human Sciences Research Council found that more than 35% of South African women experienced physical or sexual violence, many from their own intimate partners. For Bra Steve, part of the solution to the crisis is helping men to understand the issue and take responsibility for their actions. "We are a lost generation," he says. "We must restore dignity to the men around here." Amongst the group of men outside the tavern is Zizipho Mtwesi, the project co-ordinator of Father A Nation. Reflecting on recent weeks, he says more should be done. The latest measures announced by Ramaphosa, including better street lighting and a review of unsolved cases , are too little, he says, and too late. "When I think about all of these recent murders in Johannesburg, I get angry. Why do we have to wait for this to happen for us to act?" He looks around and gestures at the meeting. "We are trying to reach men before things like these murders happen again." Image source, Christian Parkinson/ BBC Image caption, Craig Wilkinson tells the group to "choose what kind of man you want to be" Craig Wilkinson is the founder of the group. "We get men to talk, to process their feelings," he explains. "And as they do, this healing takes place. And the second phase is teaching and training positive masculinity. "We ultimately hope that this will eliminate the scourge of gender-based violence." He stands up, moving into the centre of the group, calling out to the men. "You as a man are a powerful force for good," he tells them. "You choose what kind of man you want to be. Women need to be safe." Father A Nation operates across South Africa, teaching healthy masculinity and running training programmes across dozens of schools and colleges. Mystery surrounds the spate of murders which has sparked South Africa's latest moment of soul-searching about the safety of its women. Police have not ruled out potential links between some of the Ekurhuleni deaths but have not said they are investigating a serial killer. Suspects in some of the cases have appeared in court. But the spate of deaths has sparked new concerns and in Organic Market some women are more fearful than ever. Outside a nearby shack Linkie listens with interest as she cleans clothes in a large metal bucket. "We are not safe when we are outside our place," she says. "We are afraid when we see a car behind us when we walk. We feel afraid. We feel scared. What if this guy's going to kidnap me or do something to me?" It is a feeling shared by many women here. In the local hair salon, sporting a mane of thick pink braids, is Providence Maseko. She comes to the door to speak to Bra Steve. Figure caption, Women held a memorial run in Johannesburg after the discovery of Moselakgomo's body "Safety here is very bad," she says, "Maybe you are the serial killer. How do I know who to trust?" Bra Steve laughs. "We must talk about these things," he urges. "Come to our meetings and we can learn to trust each other." Maseko tells me that she now takes an e-hailing taxi everywhere in the hope that it is safer. Back at the tavern, the men's meeting is wrapping up. "As we try to stop gender-based violence," says Zizipho, "each and every man needs to know that they need to play a part in this. "And if they wouldn't allow these things to happen to their own daughters or own mothers, they mustn't allow it to be done to someone else's daughter, which is their wives or their girlfriends." Mathekga is impressed with what he has heard. "I would love them to keep on practising what we have learned, because we no longer have role models," he says. "Our fathers and our uncles, they are there in prison. We must now become role models and help make this country better." title: Could El Niño mean there are no Atlantic hurricanes this year?
body: Could El Niño mean there are no Atlantic hurricanes this year? - BBC Weather BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC Weather Menu Home Weather Warnings Flood Warnings Monthly Outlook Coast and Sea Help Could El Niño mean there are no Atlantic hurricanes this year? Image source, Getty By Simon King Lead Weather Presenter Published 3 October 2026 For the first time in more than 30 years, a hurricane has not formed in the Atlantic throughout September - normally the most active month for hurricane activity. With just two months left of the defined hurricane season, there is an increasing possibility that no hurricanes will develop at all. This would make the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season the only one in the satellite era without a hurricane. The biggest reason for this is El Niño, which traditionally stifles activity in the Atlantic but brings a very active season in the eastern North Pacific. The Atlantic hurricane season was predicted to be quieter than normal as a result of this. With a very strong El Niño forecast, the US National Hurricane Center in May predicted a total of eight to 14 named storms. Of those, three to six were predicted to become hurricanes, with one to three becoming major hurricanes. September is typically the most active month for tropical storm and hurricane activity. But, this year marks the latest date on record since the start of the satellite era (1960s onward) where no hurricane has formed in the North Atlantic. Image caption, While there have been no hurricanes forming in the North Atlantic so far this season, the Eastern North Pacific has been very active with above-average storms There were, however, four named tropical storms that formed in September: Edouard, Fay, Gonzalo and Hanna. All but Edouard stayed out in the open waters of the Atlantic. The National Hurricane Center suggests there is no sign of any tropical storm activity or hurricane over the next week at least. Forecasters at Colorado State University, who also monitor activity, suggest the strong El Niño is likely to disrupt wind patterns across the Atlantic and "likely result in below-normal activity" over the next two-weeks. As the typical peak of the season has passed and is now on a downward trend until 30 November, a season without a single hurricane is looking increasingly possible. In the historical Atlantic hurricane database,  there has not been a year without a hurricane recorded since 1914. However, this was pre-satellite monitoring so it is impossible to say with certainty that none formed. How does El Niño affect tropical development? While El Niño is the natural warming of the tropical Pacific, it can disrupt weather patterns around the globe. As wind patterns shift during an El Niño, upper winds over the Atlantic increase and this leads to more wind shear, where wind changes rapidly with height. Strong winds blowing at different speeds and directions at higher altitudes rip apart thunderstorms, preventing them from growing into tropical storms or hurricanes. Meanwhile, the Pacific typically becomes more active during El Niño because the sea surface temperatures here are much higher, combined with more favourable wind patterns. The warmer waters give storms more energy to grow into tropical storms and hurricanes. This year, temperature records have already been broken in a key region of the central-eastern Pacific, with daily sea surface temperatures now exceeding the previous record set during the very strong El Niño of 2015. There have so far been 17 named storms in the basin including nine hurricanes, seven of which were major. In terms of the amount of energy these storms have produced - known as the Accumulated Cyclone Energy - this season is around two and half times more active than normal at this point. El Niño is predicted to continue to strengthen with forecasts suggesting it will reach its peak in November or December. Federal Reserve Board announces it will extend, until November 4, the comment period on its proposal to modernize Regulation O For release at 4:00 p.m. EDT Share The Federal Reserve Board announced Friday that it will extend, until November 4, the comment period on its proposal to modernize Regulation O, its rule governing the extension of credit by a bank to its "insiders"—bank executives, board members and major shareholders who could potentially influence a bank's lending decisions. The Board extended the comment period to allow interested parties more time to analyze the issues and prepare their comments. Comments on the proposal were originally due by October 5. These investments will help secure critical supply chains, strengthen Ukraine’s energy resilience, and develop its critical mineral sector. “URIF’s first investment in March demonstrated that it was open for business. Today’s board approval of additional investments in Ukraine’s critical minerals and energy sectors signals investor support for Ukraine’s recovery and future prosperity,” said U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent .  “These investments represent the continued realization of the vision behind the novel agreement that Prime Minister Svyrydenko and I signed in April 2025 to establish URIF and give America a direct stake in Ukraine’s long-term peace and prosperity,” “Today's Board meeting marks an important step forward for the U.S.-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund. These investments strengthen Ukraine's energy resilience, develop critical mineral resources, and support innovative Ukrainian companies. Together these projects are building the foundation for Ukraine's economic recovery and deepening the partnership between our countries,” said DFC CEO Ben Black . “This round of investments shows the growing scope of the U.S.-Ukraine partnership, from energy and critical minerals to telecommunications and emerging technologies. For URIF, it is an important step in building a track record of investments that gives investors confidence in Ukraine. We want to see more Ukrainian companies develop through this partnership and create new opportunities for the Ukrainian economy,” said Oleksii Sobolev, Deputy Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine . The joint U.S.-Ukrainian URIF board of directors approved the following today: Expanding Investment in Ukraine’s Critical Minerals: URIF will establish a joint investment platform with Ukrainian company BGV Group Management. The platform will seek to build a diverse portfolio of early-stage mining projects across Ukraine, supporting the development of Ukraine’s critical minerals sector. Its initial focus will be on identified assets of rare earths, beryllium and zirconium deposits. This platform aims to significantly scale up Ukraine’s critical mineral production, creating Ukrainian jobs and investment opportunities for U.S. and Ukrainian companies and international investors, while shoring up secure supply chains of these vital critical minerals for U.S. and allied markets. Restoring Heat and Power to Ukrainian Communities: URIF’s equity investment in a multi-site distributed combined heat and power (CHP) cogeneration platform will support the construction and operation of a series of community-scale energy hubs designed to restore electricity and heat supply damaged by the war. Once completed, the project is intended to provide heat and power to thousands of households, ensuring access to vital energy and heat in Ukraine as the conflict continues. Enhancing Ukraine’s Energy Security: URIF’s debt investment provides financing for DTEK’s 200 MW/400 MWh battery energy storage system across six sites in Ukraine. The system is operational, with enough capacity to supply electricity equivalent to approximately 600,000 Ukrainian homes for two hours and provide the country’s power grid with greater resilience and stability. The project is built by DTEK, Ukraine’s largest private energy company, and leverages American energy technology at the battery storage sites to provide backup power and enable faster grid restoration. Today’s announcement comes one year after the United States and Ukraine established URIF’s initial capital base and launched the Fund’s operations, moving URIF from an institutional framework to capital deployment. The Fund made its first investment in emerging-technology company Sine Engineering in March of this year. In June, the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation signed a cooperation agreement with the Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA) to develop a political risk insurance framework that will catalyze and support private sector investment and capital mobilization in Ukraine in connection with URIF’s investments. URIF is a joint U.S.–Ukrainian investment fund and a key pillar of the economic partnership between the Trump administration and the Government of Ukraine. The Fund harnesses American and Ukrainian talent, resources, and expertise to mobilize U.S. and aligned private capital and create strategic investment opportunities in Ukraine for the United States, its allies, multilateral development banks, and private investors. URIF focuses on investments that support Ukraine’s reconstruction, supply chain resilience, and the shared economic security and prosperity of Ukraine and the United States. For more information and to submit a project proposal, please visit URIF’s website: https://urifinvest.com . title: How AI is redefining Wall Street jobs — and boosting demand for this new 'hottest skill' by 1,721%
body:
AI is redefining Wall Street jobs, boosting demand for one skill 1,721% Skip Navigation Markets Pre-Markets U.S. Markets Currencies Prediction Markets Cryptocurrency Futures & Commodities Bonds Funds & ETFs Business Economy Finance Health & Science Media Real Estate Energy Climate Transportation Investigations Industrials Retail Wealth Sports Life Small Business Investing Personal Finance Fintech Financial Advisors Options Action ETF Street Buffett Archive Earnings Trader Talk Tech Cybersecurity AI Enterprise Internet Media Mobile Social Media CNBC Disruptor 50 Tech Guide Politics & Policy White House Policy Defense Congress Expanding Opportunity Video Latest Video Full Episodes Livestream Live Audio Live TV Schedule CNBC Podcasts CEO Interviews CNBC Documentaries Digital Originals Watchlist Investing Club Trust Portfolio Analysis Trade Alerts Meeting Videos Homestretch Jim's Columns Education Subscribe PRO Pro News Josh Brown Mike Santoli Calls of the Day My Portfolio Livestream Full Episodes Stock Screener Market Forecast Options Investing Chart Investing Subscribe Livestream Menu Make It select USA INTL Livestream Search quotes, news & videos Livestream Watchlist SIGN IN Create free account Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Finance How AI is redefining Wall Street jobs — and boosting demand for this new 'hottest skill' by 1,721% Published Fri, Oct 2 2026 6:00 AM EDT Updated Fri, Oct 2 2026 2:49 PM EDT Hugh Son @hugh_son WATCH LIVE Key Points Job postings referencing "agent orchestration" exploded by 1,721% this year, making it one of the most sought-after technical skills in finance, according to an analysis by enterprise hiring data firm Draup provided exclusively to CNBC. Hiring is expanding beyond model builders to "forward-deployed engineers," who integrate AI directly into trading desks, compliance units and back-office operations. Roles tied to generative AI and agents typically pay more than tech roles elsewhere in finance, with generative AI managers paid a median base salary of about $190,000, according to Draup. In this article JPM C COF Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 2:58 02:58 Wall Street's AI hiring surges Power Lunch Before artificial intelligence can take Wall Street jobs, it is first creating them. Posts for AI-related roles at banks including JPMorgan Chase , Citigroup and Capital One surged 49% this year compared with 2025 to 139,819 listings, according to an analysis by enterprise hiring data firm Draup that was provided exclusively to CNBC. The fastest-growing area is a cluster of skills involving AI agents, according to Draup, which culls data from public job posts and platforms including LinkedIn. For instance, references to agent orchestration, or the ability to design agents that work in concert on a task, jumped 1,721% this year. "This is arguably the hottest skill on Wall Street," Draup CEO Vijay Swaminathan said in an interview. "It's a massive opportunity. They need people who understand data and people who understand AI and where to put it." The job listings show that Wall Street banks are moving beyond chatbots to the next phase of their AI strategy, one that has implications for executives, employees and shareholders. To make good on AI's promise to boost productivity and automate repetitive tasks, banks are pressing forward into a future filled with armies of agents handling an increasing share of labor. While an earlier wave of AI hiring was dominated by engineers and data scientists building models or adapting them to corporate data, the boom has expanded to include people who are responsible for embedding AI directly into business lines. Deploying AI inside a financial institution often requires stringing together multiple specialized agents: one to inspect raw data, another to analyze a document and a third to check regulatory compliance, for example. The workers involved in this process, often called forward-deployed engineers, need a combination of technical abilities and domain knowledge of a specific business or function, from trading desks to back-office operations and human resources, according to Swaminathan. "There is a lot of complexity in an enterprise," Swaminathan said. "Sometimes these complexities are visible, but many times they are hidden. It takes a long time even to automate a simple process." For instance, creating a team of agents to automate approval of employee vacation requests creates a web of edge cases and specific exemptions, he said. The agent orchestration skill is especially relevant to forward-deployed engineers, because their job is to figure out which agents are needed, what each one does and which technology to use, said the Draup CEO. It also involves deciding when human overseers need to be involved, he said. Agent tech stack Other in-demand skills related to the AI build-out involve understanding tools and techniques that give agents the ability to get things done. References to LangGraph, a framework for building multistep workflows, jumped 679%, while mentions of LlamaIndex, which helps connect AI applications to data, rose 291%, according to Draup's analysis. References to retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, a technique for feeding AI models information from company databases, climbed 259%. Beyond technical abilities, though, there is a growing emphasis on so-called soft skills. "Our analysis shows that there is a renewed focus on soft skills like problem solving, creativity, ability to ask tough questions, being assertive [when it comes to] deeper understanding of the processes," he said. Other growth areas within AI include those responsible for creating guardrails around the emerging systems, including demand for risk and control infrastructure. References in job posts tied to "responsible AI" surged 657% this year, according to Draup, while those mentioning AI governance and risk management jumped 394% and 359%, respectively. Security teams are also focused on preventing third-party tools or external model connections from creating systemic vulnerabilities. Governance-related skills now account for more than 16,000 references in the Draup data, nearly twice the roughly 8,400 tied to training, deploying and running models. "There is a lot of focus on making sure that the third parties that we are using in these products are not going rogue from a cybersecurity standpoint," he said. Roles tied to generative AI and agents typically pay more than tech roles elsewhere in finance, with generative AI managers paid a median base salary of about $190,000, according to Draup. Despite the higher pay, filling these specialized roles remains a challenge, said Swaminathan. To bridge the gap, major banks are leaning heavily into internal reskilling programs to train existing developers and domain experts, he said. The build-out will itself create ripple effects: JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimo n has spoken of " huge redeployment plans " as AI takes over more work. "I think the more we prioritize those soft skills with the right amount of technical skills, people will adapt and learn," Swaminathan said. "It's a very exciting time for the right talent." watch now VIDEO 2:43 02:43 Rashid: All companies are going to be AI companies Worldwide Exchange Choose CNBC as your preferred source on Google and never miss a moment from the most trusted name in business news. title: Spain's parliament rejects housing bill as protests continue
body: Spain's parliament rejects housing bill as protests continue Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus Israel Ethiopia German politics Latest audio Latest videos Live TV Advertisement Politics Spain Spain's parliament rejects housing bill as protests continue Mark Hallam with AFP, AP, Reuters 10/02/2026 October 2, 2026 Spain's minority government suffered defeat in parliament as it tried to push through a pair of emergency measures aimed at making housing more affordable. A pensioner's eviction and protests led to the bid. https://p.dw.com/p/5NfTv Parliamentarians voted with a crowd of protesters outside awaiting the results Image: Manu Fernandez/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Spain 's parliament has narrowly voted down a pair of emergency government decrees aiming to quell widespread protests against rising rental costs for housing. Hundreds of protesters were gathered outside the parliament in Madrid amid the marathon debate culminating in a pair of votes on Friday. They yelled "shame" and "your profits, our misery," as news of the measures being quashed filtered through. Spain has been gripped by protests for around a week , including a tent city set up in central Madrid, ignited by the eviction of an 87-year-old pensioner from her apartment that threw the more longstanding issue of unaffordable housing costs into sharp focus. Why and how did the emergency decrees fail? Left-leaning Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez leads a minority government in Spain and so relies on opposition support to legislate. Sanchez spoke at the close of a marathon 5-hour debate in the Chamber of Deputies ahead of the vote, urging members: "Do the right thing, or history will judge you, and sooner than you think." Sanchez tried to rally majority support for the measures at the last in parliament, but could not succeed Image: Eduardo Parra/Europa Press/AP Photo/picture alliance One Catalan party that sometimes supports Sanchez's government, the economically right-leaning Junts group, joined the opposition in voting down the measures. The first emergency decree, which the government said would stop evictions of vulnerable people, make real estate speculation harder and provide tax incentives to encourage renting, failed by a narrow margin of 178-172. The second decree, which sought to make residential leases automatically renewable by tenants, fell further short of a majority at 184-166. Opponents to the measures argued, among other things, that they risked compounding the situation by reducing housing supply. Some also argued that Sanchez should respond to the deadlock by calling early elections, possibly initiating a wholesale change of government. Rising rents were a sensitive issue in Spain for years, but one particularly emotive eviction brought it to the boil Image: Manu Fernandez/AP Photo/picture alliance What did protesters say after the vote? The Tenants' Union which had led protests across Spain said it would press on with plans for more mass rallies on Saturday, aiming to continue heaping pressure on the coalition and opposition alike. "The encampment will continue and will continue expanding to other neighborhoods," Tenants' Union spokesperson Alicia del Rio said. "We're aiming for a general strike." The current wave of protests, albeit concerning an issue that's been bubbling away near the surface for years, was triggered by the high-profile eviction of 87-year-old Madrid resident Maricarmen Abascal from the apartment she had occupied for almost all of her life. Maricarmen Abascal has since been granted a reprieve, but the more widespread attempts to improve the situation remain stalled for now Image: Francesco Militello Mirto/IPA/ZUMA/picture alliance How tough is Spain's housing market? The investment company owning Abascal's building reversed the measure in her case this week but only after the issue had become a symbol of growing frustration of housing costs. Rents have roughly doubled in Spain in the last decade and young people, facing one of Europe's toughest labor markets for school-leavers and graduates, frequently live with their parents past the age of 30. "People have said 'enough is enough;' this ⁠cannot ​go on. The housing problem must be resolved; structural measures must be taken, and this cannot ​continue," Abascal's lawyer, Beatriz Duro, said in an interview with Reuters on Thursday. The next step after Friday's failed vote in parliament is difficult to identify. Sanchez has so far ruled out calling early elections. He could try to formulate another emergency decree or decrees in response to the protests, but any such move would need to overcome the same hurdles in parliament. These designations expose a sophisticated, multi‑year financing architecture that moved more than $2 million to Hamas through deceptive charitable fronts and cryptocurrency channels, demonstrating the organization’s persistent ability to adapt its fundraising mechanisms to evade detection. “Terrorist organizations like Hamas rely on sophisticated financial facilitators and fraudulent schemes designed to exploit the public to sustain their operations,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent .  “Treasury will continue to identify, isolate, and impose consequences on those who provide Hamas with the financial lifelines it needs to survive.” Today’s action aligns with a broad, multi-jurisdictional operation led by the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) to dismantle several Hamas fundraising ventures, including those active inside the United States.  As part of a coordinated, whole-of-government approach which includes local law enforcement partners such as the New York Police Department, OFAC continues to work closely with the FBI to expose and disrupt Hamas’s continued exploitation of the charitable sector to finance terrorism and to dismantle key nodes of Hamas’s clandestine financial infrastructure.  Treasury will continue to sustain pressure on Hamas’s global network of financial facilitators, operatives, and sham charities that support its terrorist activities. Today’s designations were issued pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13224, as amended by E.O. 13886 (hereafter E.O. 13224, as amended), the United States’ core counterterrorism sanctions authority.  On October 31, 2001, the U.S. Department of State designated Hamas pursuant to E.O. 13224 for having committed, or posing a significant risk of committing, acts of terrorism that threaten the security of U.S. nationals, or the national security, foreign policy, or economy of the United States.  Hamas is also designated as a Foreign Terrorist Organization pursuant to section 219 of the Immigration and Nationality Act. HAMAS AL QASSAM BRIGADE MEMBER Saleem Abdallah Saleem al-Zaq ( al-Zaq ) is a Gaza-based battalion deputy in the Hamas military wing who oversees a financial network that has used various money services businesses and cryptocurrency wallets to transfer significant funds to the Hamas Al-Qassam Brigades.  He also served as a photographer in the Hamas media office and attended official Hamas events where he was afforded close proximity to senior Hamas officials, further demonstrating his trusted status within the organization. Al-Zaq is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13224, as amended, for having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Hamas. FRANCE-BASED SHAM FUNDRAISERS Faouzi Barika ( Barika ) and Amel Oualid ( Oualid ) operate from France, where they run purported charities ostensibly to raise money for humanitarian purposes to aid Gazan civilians.  In reality, they partner with al-Zaq to raise and transfer money directly to him, which al-Zaq in turn funnels to Hamas.  During a six-year period from 2020–2026, Barika, Oualid, and al-Zaq collected more than $2 million for Hamas, of which $1.5 million was collected after the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack on Israel.  Barika and Oualid sent hundreds of thousands of dollars in cryptocurrency to al-Zaq, and al-Zaq has advertised both Barika’s and Oualid’s fundraising accounts on his own social media accounts. Barika jointly established France-based Association Baraka with al-Zaq, which he uses as a mechanism to solicit public donations that are sent to al-Zaq for transfer to Hamas.  Oualid established France-based Ensemble C Mieux , which, like Association Baraka, she uses to raise money to send to al-Zaq and Hamas. Barika is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13224, as amended, for having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of, Hamas.  Oualid is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13224, as amended, for having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of, al-Zaq.  Association Baraka and Ensemble C Mieux are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13224, as amended, for being owned, controlled, or directed by, directly or indirectly, Barika and Oualid, respectively. SANCTIONS IMPLICATIONS As a result of today’s action, all property and interests in property of the designated or blocked persons described above that are in the United States or in the possession or control of U.S. persons are blocked and must be reported to OFAC.  In addition, any entities that are owned, directly or indirectly, individually or in the aggregate, 50 percent or more by one or more blocked persons are also blocked.  Unless authorized by a general or specific license issued by OFAC, or exempt, OFAC’s regulations generally prohibit all transactions by U.S. persons or within (or transiting) the United States that involve any property or interests in property of blocked persons. Violations of U.S. sanctions may result in the imposition of civil or criminal penalties on U.S. and foreign persons.  OFAC may impose civil penalties for sanctions violations on a strict liability basis. OFAC’s Economic Sanctions Enforcement Guidelines provide more information regarding OFAC’s enforcement of U.S. economic sanctions.  In addition, financial institutions and other persons may risk exposure to sanctions for engaging in certain transactions or activities involving designated or otherwise blocked persons.  The prohibitions include the making of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services by, to, or for the benefit of any designated or blocked person, or the receipt of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services from any such person.  Non-U.S. persons are also prohibited from causing or conspiring to cause U.S. persons to wittingly or unwittingly violate U.S. sanctions, as well as engaging in conduct that evades U.S. sanctions.  Individuals located in the U.S. or abroad who provide information about sanctions violations to the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network’s whistleblower incentive program may be eligible for awards if the information they provide leads to a successful enforcement action that results in monetary penalties exceeding $1,000,000. Furthermore, engaging in certain transactions involving the persons designated today may risk the imposition of secondary sanctions on participating foreign financial institutions.  OFAC can prohibit or impose strict conditions on opening or maintaining, in the United States, a correspondent account or a payable-through account of a foreign financial institution that knowingly conducts or facilitates any significant transaction on behalf of a person who is designated pursuant to the relevant authority. The power and integrity of OFAC sanctions derive not only from OFAC’s ability to designate and add persons to the SDN List, but also from its willingness to remove persons from the SDN List consistent with the law.  The ultimate goal of sanctions is not to punish, but to bring about a positive change in behavior.  For information concerning the process for seeking removal from an OFAC list, including the SDN List, please refer to OFAC’s Frequently Asked Question 897 here and to submit a request for removal, click here . title: Iran accused of blocking SIM cards, digital access to silence dissent
body: Iran accused of blocking SIM cards to silence dissent Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus Israel Ethiopia German politics Latest audio Latest videos Live TV Advertisement Freedom of Speech Iran Iran accused of blocking SIM cards to silence dissent Atefeh Chaharmahaliyan 10/02/2026 October 2, 2026 DW has spoken with several Iranians who say their SIM cards, bank access and online accounts were blocked until they deleted critical content or pledged to stop activism. https://p.dw.com/p/5NfQ0 Social media users in Iran say their SIM cards were blocked after posting political content or liking posts on Instagram Image: UGC/AFP Advertisement In Iran , cell phone numbers are a key tool for digital identity verification and access to banking, judicial, administrative and insurance services, as well as many everyday activities. As a result, disconnecting a SIM card can do more than block calls and text messages. It can also cut off access to a wide range of digital services. Some Iranians said the restrictions on their cell phones were accompanied by the blocking of user accounts and access to banking and government services. They said access was restored only after they deleted critical content or pledged to stop participating in protest-related activities . DW spoke to three people in Iran about the issue. They have used pseudonyms out of concern for their safety. 'Six hours of interrogation' Sina told DW that he realized his SIM card had been disconnected while returning from university and trying to book a taxi by phone. The 25-year-old said that after visiting a telecommunications center, he received a call from someone claiming to be from the Intelligence Organization of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IO-IRGC), who instructed him to go to a specified location to have his SIM card reconnected. A message on Instagram stating: 'The activities of the page are in accordance with the laws of the Islamic Republic of Iran' Image: unbekannt Sina said he was interrogated for about six hours and that his mobile phone was confiscated. He said the return of his SIM card and phone was made conditional on signing a pledge expressing "remorse" for his activist activities and online "propaganda against the system." He said he was also required to publish posts supporting the Islamic Republic to "prove his brotherhood with the system." Several hours later, he said, his family discovered that posts on his Instagram account had been deleted. Only one remained, stating that "the activities of the page are in accordance with the laws of the Islamic Republic of Iran." A month later, he said, he had still not received his SIM card or mobile phone back and was unable to access his social media accounts. Sorour, a 41-year-old translator at an official translation office in Tehran, said that after her SIM card was disconnected, she went to a location designated by the IO-IRGC, where she was interrogated for hours about her activities on Instagram and X. Revolutionary Guard has 'massive' role in clampdown: expert To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Sorour said she was told to make her account private and pledge to refrain from activities critical of the authorities, including advocating for political prisoners, protesting executions and supporting demonstrators during nationwide anti-government protests that began in late December 2025. Mina, who lives in Isfahan, said she was summoned by an institution she identified as the IO-IRGC after posting a comment supporting one of the country's political currents under a post by a foreign-based news outlet. The 63-year-old said her SIM card and national identification card were blocked after she refused to comply with the summons. According to Mina, the restrictions disrupted her access to bank transfers, administrative systems, online purchases and services that require electronic identity verification and one-time passwords. She told DW she had also been denied access to Sana, the judiciary's electronic system, and was therefore unable to determine whether a case or charges had been filed against her. SIM cards: the key to digital life in Iran Several other Iranian citizens also posted similar complaints on social media . Zia Nabavi, a former political prisoner, said in an Instagram post that his SIM card had been suddenly disconnected. He said he discovered the issue while at a doctor's office, where he needed access to his mobile phone and banking text messages. "For a long time, I have come to the conclusion that the government's policy toward critics and opponents is to apply pressure that pushes them toward obedience or withdrawing from their activities," Nabavi wrote. Regime 'taking the Iranian people hostage' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Reyhaneh Saeedi, a physician and activist, also said on Instagram that her SIM card has been blocked for months and that this is the second time she has faced such restrictions. She said the measure has effectively prevented her from practicing medicine, issuing prescriptions and renewing her Medical Council and medical office licenses. Saeedi said her identification card had also been deactivated. She added that no ruling had been formally served on her, she had not been informed of any charges or judicial proceedings, and her efforts to determine the reason for the restrictions had yielded no results. Actress Shaghayegh Dehghan said on Instagram that her SIM card had been blocked and that she did not know which institution or authority was behind the move. Cutting communications The disconnection of SIM cards and other digital restrictions has become part of a broader set of tools that the Islamic Republic has used over the past four decades to exert pressure on opponents, critics, journalists, and civil and human rights activists. The Defending Free Flow of Information (DeFFI) organization reported in 2025 that journalists and activists had their SIM cards blocked without judicial orders. The measures have raised concerns about the powers exercised by security institutions to deny citizens access to communication tools and essential services. They have also highlighted the absence of a clear accountability mechanism, leaving those affected with no obvious avenue to challenge the restrictions or seek an explanation. Iran cuts off internet as protests spread To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video This article was originally published in Farsi. Gemini 4 Argon leads our new frontier models with advanced reasoning for complex tasks. We’ve launched natural voice models and new app integrations to simplify your daily workflow. Exciting scientific breakthroughs include mapping human DNA and tracking global methane from space. New tools like Googlebook and Gemini for Windows help you get more done effortlessly. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Google just released a bunch of new AI updates, including the powerful Gemini 4 Argon model for solving complex problems. They’ve added cool features like better voice tools, music generation, and ways to connect your favorite apps directly into Gemini. They’re also using AI to help scientists map DNA, track climate change from space, and even study fruit fly brains. Plus, you can now use Gemini on Windows or check out their new Googlebook laptop. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Explore other styles: Bullet points Basic explainer For more than 20 years, we’ve invested in machine learning and AI research, tools, and infrastructure to build products that make everyday life better for more people. Teams across Google are working on ways to unlock AI’s benefits in fields as wide-ranging as healthcare, crisis response, and education. To keep you posted on our progress, we're doing a regular roundup of Google's most recent AI news. Here’s a look back at some of our AI announcements from September. September's headline belongs to Gemini 4 Argon, our newest frontier model. Built with advanced reasoning and a 1-million-token output limit, it’s designed to tackle complex challenges — especially in cybersecurity defense. The release capped an active month for Google AI launches that included Gemini 3.8 Flash and 3.8 Flash Cyber. We also introduced expressive voice models with Gemini 3.8 Live, made Googlebook available for pre-order, and brought the Gemini app to Windows. Beyond daily tools, we marked major scientific milestones by mapping human DNA in AlphaGenome Atlas, tracking global methane from space, and launching Project Suncatcher to test machine learning hardware in orbit. And as a nice bonus, we were grateful to see our teams’ work on designing better AI interfaces recognized by Fast Company as the 2026 Design Company of the Year. Learn about Gemini 4 Argon: our next era of frontier intelligence . Gemini 4 Argon is engineered to bring advanced reasoning to the most difficult of problems. Built with an industry-leading 1-million-token output limit, Argon excels at heavy-duty workloads like coding, cybersecurity defense, and knowledge work like financial research and legal drafting, and autonomous cybersecurity patching. Safely releasing frontier capabilities at this level requires a phased approach, and Argon is currently rolling out to trusted cyber defenders through the Fairwind Program. We’re actively gathering feedback from early testers to iterate on guardrails before expanding availability to developers, enterprises, and consumers. Get next-gen intelligence for agents and cybersecurity with Gemini 3.8 Flash and 3.8 Flash Cyber . Gemini 3.8 delivers our best reasoning and coding performance yet at the same speed and low cost as 3.7 Flash. Gemini 3.8 Flash provides substantial gains in long-horizon software engineering, multi-step problem solving, and agentic workflows. Alongside it, Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber equips defenders with frontier-grade autonomous vulnerability discovery and automated code patching — available to trusted organizations through our new Fairwind Program . Converse naturally with Gemini 3.8 Live and 3.8 Live Extended Thinking . We've launched two fast, natural language audio models: Gemini 3.8 Live for everyday conversation, and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking, the top-rated speech-to-speech model for multi-step reasoning without all the lag. Both have rolled for developers in Google AI Studio and Gemini API , and for everyone across Search Live, Gemini Live, and Google Workspace, where you can get things done using your voice in Gmail, Docs, and Keep . Say hello to Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS and Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS . Our most expressive text-to-speech models yet let you generate custom voices, direct scene dialogue, and more from simple text prompts. Instead of choosing from a fixed list of static presets, you now get a dynamic creative studio to build voice-first applications and elevate audio experiences, rolling out across products including Gemini Notebook and Google Vids. Tackle tasks with new Connected Apps in Gemini . We brought more of your favorite apps directly into Gemini, including productivity tools like Airtable, Linear, monday.com, and PandaDoc; creative platforms including Adobe, Picsart, Squarespace, and Webflow; and lifestyle services such as Peloton, SeatGeek, and Experian. Instead of switching between tabs, you can now tackle your tasks all in one place. To get started, head to your Gemini settings and select the apps you want to link. Create your best tracks yet with Lyria 3.5 in Gemini . From simple text prompts or images, you can now use our most expressive music generation model yet to produce richer arrangements, coherent songs, and personalized audio right in the Gemini app. Lyria 3.5 is available globally in Gemini and across Google AI Studio, Google Flow Music, and Google Vids. Sharpen your study routine with new Gemini Notebook tools . Now you can transform your study routine in Gemini Notebook with interactive coursework tools and animated video summaries. Master complex topics using custom flashcards, versatile quiz formats, and 60-second Short Video Overviews in over 80 languages. For back-to-school season, eligible college students can also claim a free 12-month Google AI student plan with higher usage limits. Coordinate family life effortlessly with CC in Google Labs . Google Labs is expanding CC from a personal agent into a collaborative group agent designed to handle household logistics and shared schedules. CC even gets its own email address to coordinate family calendars, track group to-dos, and streamline daily logistics in one spot with built-in privacy controls. CC for groups is now rolling out as an experimental preview in Google Labs. Learn how AI breakthroughs accelerate science and improve lives . AI is transforming theoretical science into practical, everyday impact . By accelerating life-saving therapies, forecasting natural disasters, and personalizing education, our technology delivers tangible benefits worldwide. Today, Google tools support more than 300 languages spoken by 7 billion people — reaching 86% of the global population. By open-sourcing models like MedGemma and partnering with leading research institutions, we're helping scientists make discoveries faster to improve lives everywhere. Plus, new visualizations of our AI & Economy ATLAS data make it easier to see how AI is reshaping global work, including scientific research. See how the future of AI computing could be in space . Project Suncatcher will launch its first test satellite with Planet to evaluate how Google TPUs perform under real space conditions. Satellites in low-Earth orbit can access up to eight times more solar power than on Earth, opening up new possibilities for long-term AI infrastructure. Learn questions we’re still exploring in our new four-part video series. Pre-order Googlebook, the laptop of choice for Android users . Built on Android and paired with desktop foundations from ChromeOS, Googlebook is designed for Gemini Intelligence and engineered to work with your Android phone right out of the box. New on-device AI features like Magic Pointer let you point and ask Gemini about anything on your screen with a quick cursor wiggle, while Rambler smart voice dictation instantly structures verbal brain dumps into organized, shareable notes. With no-code custom widgets and background task processing, Googlebook simplifies your daily workflow so you can get more done effortlessly. Check out WeatherNext 3, our most advanced and accurate global weather AI model . Our flagship AI weather forecasting model now includes real-time satellite data, hourly refreshes, higher resolution, precise precipitation forecasting, and clean energy variables. Plus, it’s now integrated across Search, Gemini, Maps, Google Maps Platform, and Cloud. Explore AlphaGenome Atlas: a high-resolution map of human DNA . There are billions of possible mutations in the human genome — far too many to ever test in a lab. So we introduced AlphaGenome Atlas, a database that predicts the effects of every possible single nucleotide variant in the human genome, all 9 billion of them. Designed to require zero coding skills, it’s already accelerating real-world breakthroughs in rare disease research and complex genetics. Track methane emissions globally from space . We partnered with NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory to develop MAPL-EMIT, a deep learning AI model that tracks global methane leaks from space. The model detects 50% more emissions than human experts and has already uncovered over 23,000 previously unmapped plumes, including 24 of the world's 25 largest-emitting landfills. All data is openly available on Google Earth Engine to help climate researchers and operators take faster action See five amazing visuals of the male fruit fly’s brain map . Scientists at Google, HHMI Janelia, and Cambridge University have built the first complete brain map of an adult male fruit fly, charting over 166,000 neurons and nearly 12,000 distinct cell types with the help of Google AI. By stitching together millions of microscopic images into a navigable 3D model, this research uncovers how sensory cues transform into movement. It’s a breakthrough for neuroscience that brings us closer to understanding how complex brains function. Learn about the new DeepMind Institute . The DeepMind Institute is a platform for researchers and thinkers from across Google DeepMind, Google, and the wider global research community to work on and publish creative, deeply informed ideas about a world with AGI. With AGI on the horizon, it’s incumbent on the creators of AI technology to sincerely and thoughtfully address its risks — but its transformative impact cannot be steered by technologists alone. DMI serves as a dedicated forum to spur debate, bring together diverse global voices, and build a consensus that ensures AGI benefits everyone. Access fast help on your PC with the Gemini app for Windows . Now, using the Alt + Space shortcut, you can open Gemini any time over your work to fact-check docs or brainstorm ideas without breaking your stride. In the dedicated workspace, you can delegate multi-step tasks to Gemini Spark, synthesize files across Gmail and Drive, and generate Nano Banana images or Gemini Omni videos — all in one place. title: Argentina launches cash-for-citizenship scheme
body: Argentina launches cash-for-citizenship scheme Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus Israel Ethiopia German politics Latest audio Latest videos Live TV Advertisement Politics Argentina Argentina launches cash-for-citizenship scheme Mark Hallam with Reuters 10/02/2026 October 2, 2026 Investors seeking the fastest but most costly route to Argentine citizenship can choose between a non-refundable gift of $350,000, or buying a government bond for $800,000, if they think that will pay off in the end. https://p.dw.com/p/5Ney4 Fancy an Argentine passport? The clue's in the name: it's obtainable with silver — or, more specifically, US dollars. Image: Tetiana Chernykova/Zoonar/picture alliance Advertisement Argentina 's government launched a scheme it hopes will attract wealthy investors and simultaneously "further strengthen the Argentine Republic's fiscal and financial position," offering people the chance to apply for citizenship via investment and thus bypass the more typical procedures. Economy Minister Luis Caputo and Cabinet chief Diego Santilli launched the citizenship-by-investment program amid the "Argentina Week" business event in Paris, saying it would start accepting applications during the fourth quarter of 2026. "This announcement is part of Argentina's drive toward international openness and integration, accompanied by reforms aimed at strengthening the investment climate and attracting capital," the Economy Ministry said in a statement . Argentina's President Javier Milei has tried to portray himself as a cost-cutting pro-business leader restoring stability to one of the world's most fragile economies, which has defaulted on or restructured parts of its national debt multiple times just this century. Its most recent emergency loans scheme from the IMF and World Bank was approved last April . Luis Caputo announced the move amid the 'Argentina Week' event in Paris trying to drum up business and investment Image: Teresa Suarez/AP Photo/picture alliance What are the details of the citizenship-by-investment program? The program plans to offer "two simple and transparent mechanisms" to the primary investors seeking citizenship for themselves and perhaps for their immediate family. The first is "making a direct, non-refundable contribution of $350,000 (roughly €310,000) to the National Treasury," the Economy Ministry said. The other higher risk, higher reward approach will be "subscribing to a $800,000 public bond created specifically for this program." The principal applicant's spouse and children aged 25 or under can then also apply, albeit themselves having to pay smaller fees. Spouses and childless children aged 18-25 would be charged $100,000 each, and minors would have to contribute $25,000 each. "Under this scheme, a typical family unit consisting of a principal applicant, their spouse, and two minor children could apply for Argentine citizenship for a total of $500,000," the ministry said, referring to a sum equating to well over a century earning Argentina's nominal median wage. Argentina loses 33 companies a day under Javier Milei To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Argentina said it would incorporate recommendations from the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) and the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) to ensure the adoption of international best practices and "comply with applicable standards regarding the prevention of money laundering, terrorist financing, and financial transparency." "We continue working to strengthen Argentina's ties with the world, project the value of our citizenship internationally, and consolidate the country as an open and reliable nation," Economy Minister Caputo said online.
