title: Growing fear of war in the Horn of Africa after Eritrea cuts ties with Ethiopia
body: Eritrea: Diplomatic ties collapse as Ethiopia conflict grows Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus Israel Ethiopia German politics Latest audio Latest videos Live TV Advertisement Politics Ethiopia Eritrea: Diplomatic ties collapse as Ethiopia conflict grows Silja Fröhlich 10/02/2026 October 2, 2026 The Tigray conflict is no longer just a domestic issue. As Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt trade accusations, the African Union (AU) urges restraint. Is the Horn of Africa hurtling toward a wider regional crisis? https://p.dw.com/p/5Nd2l How far across the Horn of Africa will the conflict in Ethiopia spread? Image: Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP/Getty Images Advertisement Days into Ethiopia's renewed conflict in Tigray , the frontlines appear to be expanding into the geopolitical arena. Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt are locked in a rapidly worsening diplomatic confrontation , raising fears that frictions could escalate beyond borders and draw in rival regional powers in and around the Horn of Africa. On Thursday, Addis Ababa ordered the closure of its embassy in neighboring Eritrea and expelled ten Eritrean diplomats, giving them 48 hours to leave the country. Eritrea immediately severed diplomatic ties altogether in response to the increasing crisis. Soon thereafter, Ethiopia also declared an Egyptian diplomat persona non grata, prompting Cairo to expel an Ethiopian embassy counsellor in return. This diplomatic tit-for-tat comes as fighting between Ethiopian federal forces and an opposition alliance led by the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) continues to intensify, threatening to reopen old wounds from a civil war that killed hundreds of thousands between 2020 and 2022. A resident of Dessie, located about 250 kilometers (155 miles) north of Addis in Amhara State, told DW that even beyond Tigray, the northern "region has been greatly hurt, economically and in every other aspect." On October 1, Tigrayan forces claimed victory over the towns of Abala and Erebti in the Afar region, which is yet to be confirmed Image: Tigray Peace Forces Public Relations Department Ethiopia-Eritrea: from peace to hostility The latest escalation marks a dramatic collapse in relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea. Only eight years ago, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed reopened his country's embassy in the Eritrean capital Asmara as part of a historic rapprochement with Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki. The peace agreement ended two decades of hostility, and helped Abiy earn the 2019 Nobel Peace Prize . In the 2020-2022 Tigray war, Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian forces to repel the onslaught of TPLF fighters. However, that partnership seems to have unraveled. Addis Ababa now accuses Eritrea of backing the rebel alliance in Tigray, Amhara and Afar. Ethiopia has described Eritrea's actions as outright "hostility and belligerence," as Eritrea keeps denying the allegations amid the diplomatic fallout between the two countries. Eritrean Minister of Information Yemani Meskel went as far as referring to the current tensions as a "declaration of war" by Ethiopia. This major deterioration of relations reflects deeper disputes between Addis and Asmara, which emerged long before the current fighting, in particular Ethiopia's long-running push to gain more secure access to the Red Sea. With Ethiopia being landlocked since Eritrea's split in 1993, Abiy has sought to establish sea access for years now, saying it is vital for the country's economic future and national security. Eritrea, however, has repeatedly issued warnings against any attempt to gain such access through pressure or force, as the uneasy peace between them began to fall apart. Analysts say that with the two parties now on opposing sides, Eritrea is providing rebel forces access to its Red Sea coastline, providing a lifeline to the otherwise isolated Tigray region. The new rebel alliance transforming the Tigray conflict To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Egypt: 'Reciprocity is the currency of diplomacy' The diplomatic crisis meanwhile has spread further across the region, as the Ethiopian government also started accusing Egypt and Sudan of supporting the opposition alliance. Both countries reject those accusations. Cairo responded swiftly to the expulsion of their diplomat from Ethiopia, with Egypt's Foreign Ministry spokesman summing up Cairo's position in a single sentence: "Reciprocity is the currency of diplomacy," Egypt then expelled an Ethiopian embassy counsellor in response to Addis' actions. But relations between the two countries had been strained long before the onset of the current conflict. For over a decade, Egypt has been expressing its opposition to the building of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) close to the border with Sudan, with Cairo arguing that the project could affect downstream water flows from the Nile. Against that backdrop, any deterioration in bilateral relations carries potential to reach far beyond the current conflict. Egypt and Ethiopia have repeatedly clashed over the construction of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) Image: Brian Inganga/AP Photo/picture alliance Sudan, Somalia and Gulf states also drawn into conflict Meanwhile to the west, Sudan's civil war appears to have become yet another factor in the growing regional crisis. More than three years after the start of hostilities between the Sudanese army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary group, the impoverished country remains trapped in what the UN has referred to as one of the world's worst humanitarian crises. As part of that conflict, Sudan has repeatedly accused neighboring Ethiopia of subverting the military by supporting the RSF , including reports of hosting training camps for the militias — a claim Addis Ababa rejects. To the east, Somalia continues to face its own domestic insecurity challenges from the al-Shabab insurgency and an overall sense of political instability, as Ethiopia is reportedly preparing to withdraw more than 3,000 troops from the country and redeploy them to areas affected by the fighting in the north, according to Bloomberg . At the same time, Gulf powers such as the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Saudi Arabia also keep vying for influence across the region amid unconfirmed reports of supporting various players. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed (l.) has given Somalian President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud (r.) reassurances of support in the fight against Islamism — though that arrangement might soon change (file photo from February 2025) Image: Presidency of Somalia/Anadolu/picture alliance Reports of explosions in Addis Ababa Concerns about the current escalation intensifying grew after a number of overnight explosions were reported in Addis Ababa; several diplomatic sources have since confirmed witnessing blasts in the Ethiopian capital, allegedly caused by drones. If reports that link the drone attacks to an anti-government alliance are fully verified, the attacks could be highly significant for the current outlook: Anti-government groups have never demonstrated the ability to strike Addis Ababa with drones before — especially while fighting a conflict hundreds of kilometers away in northern Ethiopia. The Ethiopian government has not publicly confirmed the claims, though the country's intelligence service announced a ban on drone flights over the capital. Shrinking hope for diplomatic solution The African Union (AU) meanwhile continues to call for restraint, attempting to pull the region back from the brink. In a statement issued after Thursday's diplomatic expulsions, the AU Commission urged Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt to resolve their differences through dialogue rather than confrontation. Amhara Region President Arega Kebede told DW that the conflict continued to cause death, displacement and economic damage. "No matter how much justification is presented, the ongoing bloodshed cannot be a sustainable answer to the region's problems," he stressed, calling on community and political figures to play a greater role in mediation efforts. Today, African leaders gather in Cairo for the Egypt-Africa Summit, providing one of the first major diplomatic forums since the latest crisis erupted. The meeting could offer an opportunity for informal discussions between regional leaders at a moment when official relations keep deteriorating rapidly. However, no major actor from within the region or outside has yet stepped forward to broker talks, as tensions across the entire Horn of Africa threaten whatever little peace and stability there remains. Press Releases The Financial Literacy and Education Commission Releases the 2026 Update to the U.S. National Strategy for Financial Literacy October 2, 2026 WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of the Treasury applauded the release of the 2026 update to the U.S. National Strategy for Financial Literacy from the Financial Literacy and Education Commission (FLEC), which is chaired by the Secretary of the Treasury and is composed of the heads of 23 federal agencies and the White House Domestic Policy Council. “The newest United States National Strategy for Financial Literacy is a roadmap to help every American build the knowledge and skills needed to achieve financial security for themselves and their families,” said Secretary Scott Bessent . “The advent of Trump Accounts demonstrates what this approach looks like in practice. By giving young Americans and their families an opportunity to save and invest together, we can make financial education tangible, help a new generation establish sound financial habits from an early age, and build the knowledge and confidence to participate in our financial markets.” 2026 Update to the U.S. National Strategy for Financial Literacy The Financial Literacy Strategy outlines the FLEC’s goals for advancing financial literacy and education across the United States and identifies priority areas and actions to help Americans build the knowledge and skills to make informed financial decisions, achieve their financial goals, and enhance their financial well-being. The Financial Literacy Strategy establishes four priority areas for the FLEC: Youth Financial Capability : Build a foundation of basic financial skills starting in childhood and young adulthood to improve financial outcomes for the next generation of Americans. Saving and Investing : Increase Americans’ knowledge of saving and investing to build financial security and achieve their financial goals, including by promoting awareness of new savings and investment vehicles such as Trump Accounts for children. Digital Financial Literacy : Improve Americans’ knowledge and decision-making skills to enable the safe and confident use of digital financial products and services. Scams and Fraud Education : Equip consumers with the knowledge to recognize and avoid scams and fraud and the tools to mitigate the impact of potential losses. The Financial Literacy Strategy also identifies best practices for delivering effective financial education, including providing actionable and timely education at key financial decision points, tailoring education to life stages and individual situations, reinforcing concepts over time, incorporating experiential and hands-on learning, supporting high-quality instruction, and evaluating program effectiveness. The Financial Literacy Strategy was developed through consultation with FLEC-represented agencies, public input, and independent research on financial literacy and education. Read Secretary Bessent’s letter as Chair of the Financial Literacy and Education Commission available here . Read the full 2026 Update to the U.S. National Strategy for Financial Literacy available here . The Financial Literacy and Education Commission The Financial Literacy and Education Commission (FLEC) was established by the Financial Literacy and Education Improvement Act, Title V of the Fair and Accurate Credit Transactions Act of 2003 (P.L. 108-159). It provides a forum for its represented Federal entities to continue coordination and collaboration that advance financial literacy and education andincrease access to financial services for all Americans. FLEC-represented agencies develop consumer-friendly, trustworthy, and consistent educational materials and tools; conduct outreach to help consumers make informed and sound decisions that enhance their financial well-being; coordinate and implement research; and develop and implement policies to improve how financial education is delivered. Learn more about FLEC and financial literacy resources at mymoney.gov . ### Latest News Bureaus Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade (TTB) Bureau of Engraving and Printing (BEP) Bureau of the Fiscal Service (BFS) Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) U.S. Mint Inspector General Sites Office of Inspector General (OIG) Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration (TIGTA) Report Scams, Fraud, Waste & Abuse Special Inspector General for Pandemic Recovery (SIGPR) U.S. Government Shared Services Administrative Resource Center (ARC)- Bureau of the Fiscal Service Treasury Direct Services for Governments Financial Management (FM) Marketplace Catalog Additional Resources Privacy Act Small Business Contacts Budget and Performance TreasuryDirect.gov Securities/Bonds Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) No FEAR Act Data Whistleblower Protection Other Government Sites USA.gov USAJOBS.gov OPM.gov MyMoney.gov Data.gov Forms.gov Regulations.gov PaymentAccuracy.gov my Social Security Vote.gov Privacy Policy Google Privacy Site Policies and Notices FAQs Feedback Careers Accessibility Contact Required Plug-ins Adobe® Reader® Twitter Facebook

body:
Jobs report September 2026: Skip Navigation Markets Pre-Markets U.S. Markets Currencies Prediction Markets Cryptocurrency Futures & Commodities Bonds Funds & ETFs Business Economy Finance Health & Science Media Real Estate Energy Climate Transportation Investigations Industrials Retail Wealth Sports Life Small Business Investing Personal Finance Fintech Financial Advisors Options Action ETF Street Buffett Archive Earnings Trader Talk Tech Cybersecurity AI Enterprise Internet Media Mobile Social Media CNBC Disruptor 50 Tech Guide Politics & Policy White House Policy Defense Congress Expanding Opportunity Video Latest Video Full Episodes Livestream Live Audio Live TV Schedule CNBC Podcasts CEO Interviews CNBC Documentaries Digital Originals Watchlist Investing Club Trust Portfolio Analysis Trade Alerts Meeting Videos Homestretch Jim's Columns Education Subscribe PRO Pro News Josh Brown Mike Santoli Calls of the Day My Portfolio Livestream Full Episodes Stock Screener Market Forecast Options Investing Chart Investing Subscribe Livestream Menu Make It select USA INTL Livestream Search quotes, news & videos Livestream Watchlist SIGN IN Create free account Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Economy Labor market faltered in September as jobs increased by just 29,000, unemployment rate rose to 4.2% Published Fri, Oct 2 2026 8:31 AM EDT Updated Fri, Oct 2 2026 9:45 AM EDT Jeff Cox @jeff.cox.7528 @JeffCoxCNBCcom WATCH LIVE Key Points Nonfarm payrolls rose by just 29,000 in September, well below the 84,000 forecast. The unemployment rate increased to 4.2%, though largely due to an influx of members in the labor force. Markets rose off the report, as traders priced in a high probability that the Fed will stay put on interest rates when it meets later in October. Wage growth slipped to its lowest annual level since May 2021. Job gains were concentrated in health care, construction and manufacturing. watch now VIDEO 4:14 04:14 Labor market faltered in September as jobs increased by just 29,000, unemployment rate rose to 4.2% Squawk Box The U.S. economy created far fewer jobs than expected in September, pointing to a surprising soft spot in the labor market and broader economy. Nonfarm payrolls rose a seasonally adjusted 29,000 for the month while the unemployment rate increased to 4.2%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones had been looking for job growth of 84,000 and an unemployment rate of 4.1%. In addition to the weakness in September, the August jobs count was revised lower to reflect a gain of 133,000 while July switched from a gain to a loss as payrolls fell by 10,000. The revisions in total showed 60,000 fewer jobs than previously reported. Market reaction was swift to the report, with traders interpreting the soft jobs numbers as good news as they likely further cemented the Federal Reserve staying put at its October meeting. Stock futures rose sharply after the release while Treasury yields slumped after recently rising to levels not seen since the early part of the century. Market-implied odds that the Fed will hold rates steady at its Oct. 27-28 meeting jumped to 82.8%, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. "For the Fed, this number should be the nail in the coffin for an October hike," Thomas Simons, chief U.S. economist at Jefferies, said in a note. "The payroll data surged in August, and we had expected the momentum to continue this month, given the historically low prints on jobless claims in recent weeks," he added. "However, it now appears that the August number was nothing more than a rebound from very weak hiring in June and July." Fed officials more closely watch the unemployment rate than the headline payrolls numbers. The household survey, which is used to calculate the jobless level, was considerably better than the establishment survey, which is used to derive the payrolls count. Household employment rose by 406,000 for the month, while the labor force swelled by 485,000 and the participation rate, which counts those working or actively searching for a job as a share of the total labor force, increased 0.2 percentage point to 61.8%, its highest since May. An alternative measure of unemployment, which includes discouraged workers and those holding part-time jobs for economic reasons, edged down to 7.6%, its lowest since January 2025. The report comes with Federal Reserve officials weighing the state of the economy and how it should affect their next interest rate move. Following statements in recent days from central bank policymakers, markets have recalibrated expectations and now expect the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee to hold off until December for its next hike. The FOMC raised benchmark rates a quarter percentage point in September. Policymakers largely see inflation as a larger threat to the economy than the labor market, which had shown resilience in recent months. The data has painted a picture of a low-hire, low-fire economy, with weekly jobless claims low and one indicator showing layoffs at their lowest rate in four years. Inflation, though, has held well above the Fed's 2% target. The most recent indicator of the central bank's preferred gauge showed core inflation at a 3% annual rate. Wages, though, continued to show signs of disinflation. Average hourly earnings increased just 0.1% in September, putting the 12-month gain at 3%, the lowest since May 2021. Wall Street had been looking for readings of 0.3% and 3.1%, respectively. The average work week was unchanged at 34.6 hours. "Americans are frustrated by the lack of opportunities right now," said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. "Wage growth fell to a new 5-year low and is being wiped out entirely by inflation. That stings heading into the holidays." However, Long described the labor market as "stable" and said she doesn't think the Fed will be dissuaded from hiking in December. Most of the monthly job gains came from healthcare, which added 17,000 workers. Construction was up by 11,000, and manufacturing added 9,000. Government employment fell by 17,000, while temporary help services saw a decline of 11,000, and information services lost 10,000 amid worries over the impact artificial intelligence may have on the jobs picture. Financial activities also saw a drop of 7,000 jobs. The weak job growth comes despite signs of strength elsewhere. On a macro level, economic growth has been strong. Earlier this week, the Commerce Department revised its count of both first- and second-quarter gross domestic product growth, to 2.5% and 2.2%, respectively. title: Why UK diesel prices have breached the £2 per litre mark
body: Why UK diesel prices have breached the £2 per litre mark - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat Business New Tech Economy Artificial Intelligence Technology of Business Africa Business Paths to Success Why UK diesel prices have breached the £2 per litre mark Image source, Maskot/Getty Images Published 2 March 2026 Updated 2 October 2026 The price of diesel in the UK has breached the £2 per litre mark for the first time, as the fallout from the US-Israel war with Iran continues to drive up costs. The average price of a litre of diesel at the pump stands at an all-time high of 200.01p, according to the RAC motoring body. Over the past seven months, the Iran war has severely disrupted the production and transportation of oil across the region, causing the price of fuels made from crude to surge. Motor fuel prices fell back when the US and Iran agreed in June to a framework deal to end the fighting, but rose again as tensions resurfaced. Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump has responded to rising prices by mulling a ban on US diesel producers selling overseas - a move which could push UK prices even higher. How do oil prices affect the cost of petrol and diesel at the pump? Crude oil is a key ingredient in petrol and diesel, which means that higher wholesale costs make filling up a car more expensive. The price of petrol and diesel is also heavily influenced by demand and refining capacity. Analysts say every $10 (£7.55) per barrel increase in the oil price pushes up pump prices by roughly 7p a litre. Since the Iran war began, the price of a barrel of Brent crude – the global benchmark for wholesale oil prices – has been very volatile. Generally speaking, news of further conflict drives the price up while hopes of an end to the war pushes the price down. Before the Middle East conflict, Brent was trading just over $70 a barrel but the fighting saw it peak at above $120. In early July, after the framework deal was signed, prices fell back to near the $70 mark. The price climbed back up again after peace talks collapsed and it is now around $100 a barrel. Why has the Iran war had a big impact on oil prices? A lot of oil is produced in the Middle East, and the conflict has severely disrupted the production and the transportation of it, causing its price to jump. Of particular concern to wholesale oil traders was Iran's effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz - a vital waterway south of the country through which one fifth of the world's oil and gas usually flows. There are signs that wholesale oil transport through the strait is returning to pre-war levels, but wholesale prices remain high because traders fear this might not last. Meanwhile, the transportation of refined oil products, such as car and plane fuel, remains down because of damage to refineries in the region and because refined products are more flammable, making them more dangerous to move during a conflict. What has happened to petrol and diesel prices in the UK? Before the war began, the average price of petrol was 132.83p per litre and diesel was 142.38p, according to the RAC. Diesel is now 200.01p, the highest on record. Meanwhile, petrol has hit an average 174.71p a litre, which is the highest in more than four years but lower than its peak of 191.5p during the summer of 2022. Simon Williams, head of policy at the RAC, said prices at the pumps will not come down until there is a "sustained lower oil price - over several weeks, not days". Because transporting oil is a slow process, price movements in wholesale oil markets take about a fortnight to show at the pump. Fuel retailers have denied accusations of price gouging during the conflict. The official markets regulator said it had "not seen evidence of retailers actively changing their pricing strategies to take advantage of the crisis". A government scheme called Fuel Finder , external lets drivers compare the cost of fuel offered by petrol stations across the UK. In May, the then Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer said a planned 5p increase in fuel duty due in September would be postponed until the end of December because of the conflict. Williams said that the UK government has "limited leverage when it comes to ending the US/Iran war" but lowering fuel duty further or reducing VAT could "ease the burden" at home. How might higher diesel prices affect me? Even if you don't drive a diesel car, you could still be hit by the rise in diesel prices. That's because diesel is used heavily in agriculture and, crucially, in haulage. So transporting some of our biggest essentials – particularly food – around the country is getting more expensive. Previous episodes of high costs at the pumps have even had a knock-on effect on school transport and trips, putting pressure on councils and schools, particularly in rural areas. No evidence of widespread fuel price-gouging, watchdog says Published 1 May Drivers can compare fuel prices at different petrol stations - how does it work? Published 2 February What would happen if the US banned diesel exports? While Trump has suggested he might ban US producers from selling diesel overseas, he has not done it yet and views differ on how serious this threat is. If it does happen, many agree it would hurt the countries which heavily depend on US diesel. One such country is the UK, which depends on the US for around 17% of its diesel supplies. Other European countries also import a lot of US diesel. As such, many worry any ban could drive UK diesel prices up even further. And while the ban would be likely to reduce US diesel prices in the short-term, experts say it could have unintended effects that could hurt US production – and put pressure on US diesel prices – in the long-term. Why does diesel cost more than petrol in the UK? In the UK, we have four refineries. Between them, they make more than enough petrol to meet our needs, so we sell the rest as export. However, they don't make enough diesel, which means we rely on imports. The closure last year of refineries in Grangemouth and Immingham has increased that reliance, meaning we now buy over half of our diesel from overseas. In addition, the cost of importing diesel has risen because of Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Although the UK has stopped buying Russian diesel in response to the war, other countries have carried on, meaning you have "more countries competing for less diesel", the RAC's Williams says. All of this then feeds through to prices at the pump, with diesel costing much more than petrol in the UK and the gap having widened over the last few years. title: North and South Korea trade accusations over landmines that injured three soldiers
body: Is North Korea pushing the limits of the DMZ? Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus Israel Ethiopia German politics Latest audio Latest videos Live TV Advertisement Conflicts North Korea Is North Korea pushing the limits of the DMZ? Julian Ryall 10/02/2026 October 2, 2026 A mine blast that injured three South Korean soldiers has renewed scrutiny of North Korea's actions along the border and raised questions about its strategic goals. https://p.dw.com/p/5NaaE North Korea has been fortifying the border after a shift in policy against Seoul, calling it a 'foe' [FILE: June 2019] Image: Ahn Young-joon/AP/picture alliance Advertisement Pyongyang and Seoul are trading increasingly hostile accusations across the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) that divides the peninsula, 10 days after three South Korean soldiers were injured by a land mine on the South's side of the border. The latest tensions may reflect a broader North Korean effort to test South Korea 's resolve while extending its control to the outer limits of its territory, including an area that has effectively been a no-man's land for more than 70 years, according to a professor of foreign policy at South Korea's Kyung Hee University. "The North revised its constitution in March this year and officially stated that they intend to define the absolute geographical limits of the nation, and that includes within the DMZ," said Choo Jae-woo. "They want to maximize their territory and it is my sense that they would like to push the Military Demarcation Line [MDL] — the half-way point in the DMZ — further south," he told DW. "I see the placing of landmines on the South's side of the line as a purely political act by the North, an attempt to threaten and intimidate the South." Why Seoul blames North Korea The three men were part of an 18-strong patrol clearing a new route through the DMZ as part of an investigation into the activities of North Korean troops in the western sector of the zone. The four-kilometer-wide strip of land has divided the peninsula since the Korean War ended in an armistice in 1953. The DMZ is a fortified buffer zone between the two Koreas that has been in place since 1953 Image: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance Shortly before 11 a.m. on September 21, the patrol was around 10 meters south of the MDL when a staff sergeant detonated a mine. A second mine went off as the unit commander approached to provide assistance. Both men were successfully evacuated and have undergone surgery, with a third soldier treated for minor wounds. The South Korean military has conducted an investigation with the United Nations Command, which administers the armistice on the border, and concluded in a report released this week that the mine was of North Korean origin. The Joint Chiefs of Staff on Wednesday accused the North of sowing mines to the south of the MDL, a breach of the armistice agreement, and demanded an apology from Pyongyang and a commitment to halt the construction of further fortifications along the border. "This constitutes a blatant violation of the Armistice Agreement and undermines the spirit of existing inter-Korean agreements and must be halted immediately," Kang Hyun-woo, chief director of operations, said in a press briefing. "North Korea must immediately cease activities that heighten tensions on the Korean Peninsula, such as its so-called 'border fortification.' We strongly demand an apology and responsible measures from the North," Kang added. In a statement, the UN Command said it had "determined that an Armistice Agreement violation occurred. UNC is addressing the violation through established Armistice mechanisms." Prisoner swap: From North to South Korea via Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Many in the South are demanding more resolute action on the grounds that failure to respond will be taken as a sign of weakness in Seoul. Na Kyung-won, a politician from the conservative opposition People Power Party (PPP), has demanded that the South Korean military carry out exercises simulating a "decapitation attack" against North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. She has also called for the restart of propaganda broadcasts from loudspeakers on the border and for dissident groups to be allowed to launch balloons carrying propaganda into the North. A pattern of border confrontations Yu Yong-weon, also of the PPP, told reporters on Wednesday that North Korean troops had crossed the MDL around 20 times in August and on 30 occasions in September. On each occasion, South Korean troops fired warning shots when the incursions were detected. An editorial in the Korea JoongAng Daily on Thursday said North Korea must be "held accountable" for the incident, arguing that Pyongyang's denial of responsibility "demands a firm response, clear accountability and stronger border enforcement." Kim Jong Un's sister Kim Yo Jong has accused Seoul of conspiracy after it blamed Pyongyang for the blast in the DMZ Image: Yuri Smityuk/TASS/dpa/picture alliance The North is not backing down, however, with Kim Yo Jong , sister of leader Kim Jong Un, accusing the South of staging a provocation and threatening to retaliate. In a statement published by the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) on Wednesday, Kim Yo Jong dismissed the South's allegations as a "self-staged farce" and accused the "South Korean armed gangs" of using the incident to justify political and military provocations against Pyongyang. Accident or calculated provocation? Andrei Lankov, a professor of history and international relations at Seoul's Kookmin University, is more willing to view the landmine detonations as an accident. "It makes no sense to me for North Korea to do this deliberately," he said. "At the moment, the North wants to keep a low profile and do nothing that could provoke the South. There is no gain in a deliberate attack like this." Lankov believes a more likely scenario is that the mines were shifted from the northern side of the MDL in heavy rain or natural movements of the terrain, meaning that the North's protestations of innocence are genuine. "I also do not think the South Korean government has any interest in escalating the situation further and that they will hope this is quickly forgotten," he said. "They will want to brush it under the carpet." Choo, however, is less convinced and senses a growing anger in South Korean society that the government is not standing up to provocations from north of the border. "I believe that resuming the propaganda broadcasts over the border would be an effective response, but I do not believe this government will do that," he said. "This government is trying very hard to connect with the North, but I see a failure to take a firm line this time being interpreted in the North as a sign of weakness in Seoul. "Not responding would give Pyongyang a green light to push a little more and then a little more again," he said. "There is a lot of anger here that the government is not doing enough to protect soldiers who are serving on the DMZ, to protect the people and to protect our territory." A television station broadcasts Kevin Warsh, chairman of the US Federal Reserve, speaking after a Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting as a trader works on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York, US, on Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images Investors now think the odds are extremely unlikely that the Federal Reserve raises interest rates again in October, following a weaker-than-expected September employment report . CME's FedWatch tool, based on trading in 30-day interest rate futures, shows only a 17% chance that the Fed increases rates by a quarter percentage point. One week ago, odds were close to 36%. On prediction market platform Kalshi, chances for a hike in October stood at just 18%, down from almost 70% a week ago. The U.S. economy added only 29,000 jobs in September, below estimates for a gain of more than 80,000. A softer labor market could recalibrate the Fed's thinking in how it balances its dual mandate to ensure full employment and steady prices, after it raised interest rates at its September meeting to combat inflation that's remained above target for five years . Odds for a hike in October also fell in the middle of this week after the release of the personal consumption expenditures price index , the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, on Wednesday showed cooler-than-expected prices. Core prices, excluding food and energy, rose 3% in August, lighter than consensus estimates for a rise of 3.3%. "This report strengthens the case for the Federal Reserve to remain patient," said Adam Schickling, a senior economist at Vanguard. "The labor market has not deteriorated sharply, but there is also little evidence that it has meaningfully strengthened, giving policymakers reason to wait for additional data." While traders now think a hike in October is unlikely, they're still forecasting that the central bank will raise rates in December. On FedWatch, odds are above 75% for a hike in December, while on Kalshi there are 65% odds that the Fed raises rates. The Federal Reserve is set to announce its next decision on interest rates at the conclusion of a two-day policy meeting on Oct. 28. — CNBC's Michelle Fox contributed reporting Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment. title: NVIDIA DGX Spark 64GB Gives Developers More Ways to Build and Scale Local AI
body: NVIDIA DGX Spark 64GB Gives Developers More Ways to Build and Scale Local AI | NVIDIA Blog Skip to content NVIDIA DGX Spark 64GB Gives Developers More Ways to Build and Scale Local AI Starting Friday, Oct. 23, the new configuration will be available from Acer, ASUS, Dell, Gigabyte, HP and MSI; plus, NVIDIA Sync Cluster Assistant scales projects and workloads seamlessly. October 2, 2026 by Allen Bourgoyne 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! Local AI is becoming more useful by the token. As AI agents move from experiments into everyday development, increasingly capable open models are shrinking to fit on more devices, giving builders more to run locally. Coming this month, NVIDIA DGX Spark will be available with 64GB of unified memory from top manufacturer partners — Acer, ASUS, Dell, Gigabyte, HP and MSI — giving developers, researchers and AI enthusiasts a new configuration with DGX OS and the NVIDIA AI software stack ready to use from day one. The new SKU runs capable local agents on device — privately, without cloud dependency. And when workloads grow, two units can cluster together via NVIDIA Sync Cluster Assistant without any additional setup. A New Starting Point for Personal AI Supercomputing DGX Spark combines NVIDIA Grace Blackwell compute, unified memory, NVIDIA ConnectX-7 networking and an NVIDIA CUDA -accelerated AI software stack in one system. It’s a complete local AI platform for agents, inference, fine-tuning, data science and edge development. The compact, personal AI supercomputer provides a place to experiment with models and developers’ own data without turning to a cloud instance for every task. The new 64GB configuration, available exclusively from manufacturer partners, keeps the platform at an accessible price point while retaining the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip, DGX OS and full NVIDIA AI software stack — same as the 128GB model. It supports up to 100-billion-parameter models and the agentic applications built on them, fully on device. Two 64GB units clustered together don’t just double the memory. In NVIDIA’s Qwen 3.8 27B test, two clustered 64 GB systems delivered up to 1.7x performance compared with a single system, with room to keep scaling as workloads demand. DGX Spark ships ready for agent development from day one — NVIDIA Agent Toolkit, CUDA-X AI libraries, Nemotron open models, and popular runtimes like Ollama, vLLM, and PyTorch with CUDA are all supported out of the box. Developers can go from power-on to running models in minutes. Blender is among the first major creator application providers to support the platform, with a prebuilt, downloadable installer coming soon . Scale Up With NVIDIA Sync Cluster Assistant Developers can start with the memory their projects need today and build on a platform designed to seamlessly scale multi-node clusters for larger workloads as their pipelines grow. Every DGX Spark ships with a built-in NVIDIA ConnectX-7 NIC right out of the box. Plus, two units can connect directly with a QSFP cable, pooling their memory to 128GB and expanding model support to up to 200 billion parameters while delivering twice the memory bandwidth and up to 1.7x the performance. The NVIDIA Sync app configures this multi-node cluster seamlessly. The cluster assistant feature detects connected units, validates device configuration and configures the ConnectX-7 network, so developers can focus on their work rather than the infrastructure. Every node runs the same NVIDIA software stack, so nothing needs to be reconfigured when scaling from one unit to two. And coming at the end of the month, NVIDIA Sync Model Launcher makes running local AI as simple as clicking a few buttons. Developers can download and launch Qwen3.8 27B on a single DGX Spark system or a cluster, with NVIDIA Sync configuring the model to run across connected devices and making it accessible from users’ laptops. The launcher will also set up OpenCode to use the model, so developers can start coding in their browser. Developer Use Cases on DGX Spark The new DGX Spark 64GB configuration supports practical work from day one. With up to 100-billion-parameter models running entirely on device, developers and enthusiasts can start with a single system for models that fit within its memory, or connect multiple DGX Spark systems with NVIDIA Sync Cluster Assistant for workloads that need more memory and compute. Here are three workflow examples: Run an AI agent around the clock: Keep a coding or research agent running on DGX Spark, ready to review code, analyze documents or carry out multistep tasks. A cluster provides additional capacity for larger models, longer context windows or multiple agents working at once. Power AI apps on your everyday PC: Run a language- or image-generation model on DGX Spark while using an agent or creative application on laptops or desktops. DGX Spark handles the model inference, freeing PCs for other work. Scale when the work grows: When a single task outgrows one unit — running a larger model, a longer context window or concurrent agent requests — two DGX Spark 64GB systems connected over the 200 GbE fabric via NVIDIA Sync Cluster Assistant pool their memory to 128GB. The same workflow that ran on one unit scales to two without reconfiguring the software environment. Get Started With DGX Spark DGX Spark 64GB is available from Acer , ASUS , Dell, Gigabyte , HP and MSI on Friday, Oct. 23, starting at $4,999. To get started: Download a supported inference framework — llama.cpp, Ollama, vLLM or LM Studio. Download the recommended local model for the workflow. To scale to two units, connect them via their NVIDIA ConnectX-7 ports and launch NVIDIA Sync Cluster Assistant — it configures the network and routes workloads automatically. For agentic AI playbooks on DGX Spark, visit the NemoClaw , OpenClaw , Hermes Agent and OpenShell pages on build.nvidia.com. #ICYMI: More Updates From NVIDIA Local AI Explore playbooks on build.nvidia.com/spark for DGX Spark. The following playbooks are coming soon to 64GB devices: Serve LLMs With vLLM Run OpenClaw With a Local LLM Connect Multiple DGX Sparks for Distributed Workloads New Windows PCs powered by NVIDIA RTX Spark are coming this month from Acer, ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI. Sign up for the RTX Spark newsletter to receive future updates. Alibaba’s Qwen-Image-2.1 brings image generation and editing together in a lightweight, open-weight model. It runs locally on NVIDIA RTX GPUs, DGX Spark and DGX Station, giving creators more ways to create and refine images on their own hardware. Follow NVIDIA RTX Spark on X , Instagram , TikTok and Facebook — and stay informed by subscribing to the NVIDIA Local AI newsletter . Follow NVIDIA Workstation on LinkedIn and X . Fixed-term employee Short-term employee Trainee Cost-free secondee FAQs Search Menu ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Search Options Image Preview Sort by ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Suggestions Home Media Explainers Research & Publications Statistics Monetary Policy The €uro Payments & Markets Careers Suggestions Sort by Relevance Date Decisions taken by the Governing Council of the ECB (in addition to decisions setting interest rates) August-September 2026 2 October 2026 External communication Announcements related to the digital euro project On 30 July 2026 the ECB issued a press release outlining the accessibility features of the digital euro app, the design of which will go beyond the requirements set out in the European Accessibility Act , and announcing that the ECB would start usability and accessibility testing as part of the digital euro pilot in 2027. The press release, together with the related underlying documentation, is available on the ECB’s website. On 15 September 2026 the ECB issued a call for expression of interest inviting e-commerce and mobile commerce (m-commerce) merchants operating in the euro area to take part in the digital euro pilot . The deadline to submit applications is 27 October 2026. Finally, on 28 September 2026 the ECB issued another call for expression of interest inviting private companies and organisations to collaborate in exploring how the digital euro infrastructure could support them in their innovation efforts. More detailed information is available in the related announcement published on the ECB’s website. The deadline to submit applications is 9 November 2026. Strong participation in the ECB survey on the future design of the euro banknotes On 23 September 2026 the ECB issued a press release reporting that almost ten million people across Europe and beyond had completed the ECB survey on the future design of euro banknotes, which ran between 23 July and 21 September 2026. This level of participation, equal to 2.6% of the euro area population, is unprecedented for such a survey. The press release also outlined the next steps in the process. More information on the future banknotes, the shortlisted proposals and the selection process is available on the ECB’s website. Market operations Amendments to legal acts on the implementation of the Eurosystem monetary policy framework On 22 September 2026 the Governing Council adopted amendments to the legal acts implementing the Eurosystem monetary policy framework. The amending legal acts are Guideline ECB/2026/26 amending Guideline (EU) 2015/510 on the implementation of the Eurosystem monetary policy framework and Guideline ECB/2026/27 amending Guideline (EU) 2016/65 on the valuation haircuts applied in the implementation of the Eurosystem monetary policy framework. The amendments will apply from 30 November 2026 and include the changes detailed in a related press release available on the ECB’s website. Macroprudential policy and financial stability Response of the European System of Central Banks (ESCB) to the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCAR) targeted consultation On 7 September 2026 the Governing Council, with the involvement of the General Council, approved the ESCB’s response to the European Commission’s targeted consultation on the review of MiCAR. The response , which welcomes the consultation to assess areas where existing rules could be improved with a view to ensuring that MiCAR remains fit for purpose, taking into account lessons learned from the initial years of MiCAR’s implementation, evolving market dynamics and practices in other jurisdictions, is available on the ECB’s website. Market infrastructure and payments Appointment of a new member of the Market Infrastructure Board (MIB) On 30 July 2026 the Governing Council approved the appointment of Sigríður Dis Guðjónsdóttir, Head of Payments and Resilience at the Central Bank of Iceland, as a non-voting member of the MIB from a non-euro area central bank until 31 May 2029. The full list of members of the MIB is available on the ECB’s website. Agreement for and go-live of the Pontes pilot On 11 August 2026 the Governing Council approved an agreement governing the initial launch of Pontes, a solution that enables wholesale transactions in tokenised assets to be settled in central bank money. The agreement between the Eurosystem central banks and the solution-providing Eurosystem national central banks establishes a binding legal framework for a production grade system while, at the same time, reflecting the interim nature of this phase of the service. It also includes terms and conditions for market participants and market distributed ledger technology (DLT) operators that will provide contract templates for arrangements between the Eurosystem central banks and their market participants and market DLT operators. On 11 September 2026 the Market Infrastructure Board recommended proceeding with the scheduled Pontes initial launch date of 21 September 2026. A related press release is available on the ECB’s website. ECB Decision on the identification of Visa Europe Payment System as a systemically important payment system On 24 August 2026 the Governing Council adopted Decision ECB/2026/22 on the identification of the Visa Europe Payment System as a systemically important payment system pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2025/1355 on oversight requirements for systemically important payment systems. The Decision, which was notified to the German branch of Visa Europe Limited in its capacity as operator of Visa Europe Payment System for the euro area, is available on EUR-Lex. As a result of the Decision, Visa Europe Payment System will be overseen by the Eurosystem with the ECB acting as lead overseer. Progress update on the interlinking of TARGET Instant Payment Settlement (TIPS) with other fast payment systems On 24 September 2026 the Governing Council took note of a status update on progress made on interlinking the TIPS platform with other fast payment systems globally and approved the initiation of an assessment of the feasibility of interlinking with Brazil’s instant payment system, Pix. A related article is available on the ECB’s website. The Governing Council also considered a recommendation of the Market Infrastructure Board on the pricing of the TIPS interlinking service. More detailed information will be provided on the ECB’s website as further progress is made. Advice on legislation ECB Opinion on the Polish Defence Investment Fund On 28 July 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/23 at the request of the Marshal of the Polish Parliament. ECB Opinion on Ireland's participation in the International Monetary Fund’s Resilience and Sustainability Trust On 12 August 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/24 at the request of the Irish Minister for Finance. ECB Opinion on the introduction of a ban on crypto-asset activities, and measures concerning the application of Regulation (EU) 2023/1114 On 12 August 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/26 at the request of the Marshal of the Polish Parliament. ECB Opinion on rules concerning the conduct and integrity of staff members of a supervisory authority and of the members of its executive board On 14 August 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/25 at the request of the German Federal Ministry of Finance. ECB Opinion on supervisory independence and prevention of conflicts of interest On 19 August 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/27 at the request of the Luxembourg Ministry of Finance. ECB Opinion on the objectives of the Financial Supervisory Authority, restricted authorisations of credit institutions and amalgamations of credit institutions On 31 August 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/28 at the request of the Finnish Ministry of Finance. ECB Opinion on the prevention of conflicts of interests of the Governor, Deputy Governor and employees of the Central Bank of Cyprus On 21 September 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/29 at the request of the Minister for Justice and Public Order of Cyprus. Corporate governance Extension of mandate of two Administrative Board of Review (ABoR) members and one alternate On 11 September 2026 the Governing Council decided, in line with Article 24(2) of the SSM Regulation, to extend for an additional full term of five years the mandates of Christiane Campill as ABoR member and of Damir Odak as ABoR alternate until 30 November 2031, as well as the mandate of Pentti Hakkarainen as ABoR member until 31 January 2032. The mandates of the other three members of the ABoR, the body carrying out internal administrative reviews of decisions taken by the ECB in the exercise of its supervisory powers, will expire in 2029. More detailed information on the ABoR is available on the ECB’s banking supervision website. Opinion of the Ethics Committee on the envisaged post-employment activity of a member of the Governing Council On 24 September 2026 the Governing Council concurred with the opinion of the Ethics Committee that the intention of Ms Isabel Schnabel, member of the Executive Board and Governing Council of the ECB, to take up the position of Financial Counsellor and Director of the Monetary and Capital Markets Department at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) as of 4 January 2027 did not raise, and could not be perceived as raising, conflict of interest concerns. Therefore, the Ethics Committee concluded that no cooling-off period applied in this case. On the same day, Ms Schnabel resigned from her position at the ECB with effect from 3 January 2027. A related press release is available on the ECB’s website. Statistics Amending Guideline on balance sheet item statistics and interest rate statistics of monetary financial institutions (MFIs) On 11 September 2026 the Governing Council adopted Guideline ECB/2026/25 amending Guideline ECB/2021/11 on balance sheet item statistics and interest rate statistics of monetary financial institutions. The amendments are of a technical nature, introducing, for instance, updates to the reporting of quarterly statistical information on loans to non-financial corporations to ensure their alignment with the revised statistical classification of economic activities in the European Union (NACE). ECB Banking Supervision Decision setting out the data protection arrangement for the processing of personal data in the context of supervision On 30 July 2026 the Governing Council did not object to a proposal by the Supervisory Board to adopt Decision ECB/2026/18 on the processing of personal data in the context of the prudential supervision of credit institutions. The Decision, available on EUR-Lex, sets out the allocation of the respective roles and responsibilities between the joint controllers, which are the ECB and the national competent authorities (NCAs), for compliance with Regulation (EU) 2018/1725, concerning the ECB, and Regulation (EU) 2016/679, concerning the NCAs, when processing personal data in carrying out a number of key supervisory tasks. Publication of the results of the 2026 geopolitical risk reverse stress test On 31 July 2026 the ECB published the results of its 2026 geopolitical risk reverse stress test, covering 110 euro area banks directly supervised by the ECB. The results , together with a related press release , are available on the ECB’s banking supervision website. Annual Report on whistleblowing activities in the SSM in 2025 On 4 August 2026 the Governing Council did not object to a proposal by the Supervisory Board to publish the first annual report on whistleblowing activities in the Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM). The report, which covers the year 2025, is aimed at providing the general public with an overview of SSM-wide whistleblowing activities conducted in the context of prudential supervision. It summarises, in an aggregated manner, information on whistleblowing reports received by the relevant authorities in 2025, including the follow-ups. The report is available on the ECB’s banking supervision website. ECB compliance with the EBA Guidelines on amending Guidelines on the application of the definition of default under Article 178 of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 On 14 August 2026 the Governing Council did not object to a proposal by the Supervisory Board to notify the European Banking Authority (EBA) that, for the significant institutions under its direct supervision, the ECB already complies with the amended EBA Guidelines on the application of the definition of default under Article 178 of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 ( EBA/GL/2026/05 ). Delegation frameworks for decisions regarding the assessment of group recovery plans and decisions regarding material changes to rating systems for calculating own funds requirements for credit risk and amending Decision on the delegation of power to adopt decisions on internal models and on extension of deadlines On 21 August 2026 the Governing Council adopted Decision (EU) 2026/2036 on delegation of the power to adopt decisions on material changes to rating systems for calculating own funds requirements for credit risk ( ECB/2026/19 ), Decision (EU) 2026/2037 amending Decision (EU) 2021/1442 on delegation of the power to adopt decisions on internal models and on extension of deadlines (ECB/2021/38) ( ECB/2026/20 ) and Decision (EU) 2026/2038 on delegation of the power to adopt joint decisions on the assessment of group recovery plans ( ECB/2026/21 ). These legal acts are intended to enhance the performance of the ECB’s supervisory tasks considering the considerable number of decisions taken in these areas. On the basis of these Decisions, on 1 September 2026 the Executive Board adopted Decision (EU) 2026/2039 nominating heads of work units to adopt joint decisions on the assessment of group recovery plans ( ECB/2026/23 ) and Decision (EU) 2026/2040 nominating heads of work units to adopt delegated decisions on material changes to rating systems for calculating own funds requirements for credit risk ( ECB/2026/24 ). title: School protests send shivers down French government's spine
body: French school protests send shivers down the government's spine - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East School protests send shivers down French government's spine Figure caption, Watch: Why are students staging protests at schools in France? By Hugh Schofield Paris correspondent Published 2 October 2026 It is a piece of wisdom that all French leaders take care to heed: young people on the street equals trouble. Since the student protests of May 1968 – memorably described by President De Gaulle as chienlit (bed defecation, in other words chaos) – every government has run scared of angry French youth. Why? Because youth movements are unpredictable and shapeless, often with no clear structure to negotiate with. Because when they protest, other groups join in. Also: because as they're young, the public tends to sympathise. And because if the police mess up and cause injury or worse, then the consequences are incalculable. And presidential elections are only months away. For all these reasons, when la jeunesse en colère (angry youth) is at the barricades governments tread very carefully indeed. Right now, French teenagers are at the barricades and if they are not visibly angry (the mood is more excitement), they certainly have the government of President Emmanuel Macron in what Le Monde called on Friday "the cold sweats". A movement that started nearly two weeks ago in the low-income Seine-Saint-Denis area of northern Paris has in the last few days spread across the country. Live: Fires lit on streets across France after student protests force hundreds of schools to close On Thursday – the high point so far – hundreds of lycées (where 15-18 year-olds finish their schooling) were being blockaded. On Friday, the situation had improved but around 400 lycées were closed in order to protect staff and students.  Universities are beginning to join in. Violence has erupted. On Thursday the main hall of a lycée in Nantes was destroyed by fire. Smaller fires too numerable to mention were lit at school entrance gates around the country. The cost of the damage is millions of euros. According to Education Minister Édouard Geffray, 65 teaching staff including 40 school heads have been injured. "Most of the staff who were hurt said that the people they were facing… were not their own pupils," he said. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Since the infamous protests of 1968, French governments have known the power of young people taking to the streets In addition, the government says that around 300 police and firefighters have been treated for injuries, and some 2,000 people – mainly minors – taken into custody. For their part, student groups say they have a long list of people injured by police. Two teenagers have serious eye injuries and one has lost many of his teeth. The problem would be hard enough if it was just a question of meeting the protesters' demands. But there is another dimension – a political and social one – which makes this student crisis far more dangerous than in the past. The demands do exist, even if they remain vague. They are about money – the lack of it – and the need for more teachers, smaller classes and better buildings. On such matters, many in France would agree with the teenagers. Certainly using protest to demand money from government is such a national habit that even governments agree it's legitimate.   And of course, things are indeed getting worse in the education system – because money is so tight. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The protests have spread across France, and some university students are now joining in This week Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu published his draft for next year's budget. The motif is "More cuts – and this time we're serious!" Whether or not he manages to remove €54bn (£46bn) from state spending, as he promises, remains open to question. But it is surely obvious that the era of public largesse to defuse social unrest in France is now in its twilight. Students demanding an extra school nurse or insulation in the dining-block are likely to be disappointed. But that is the lesser of the worries. The far greater fear is that these student protests are being manipulated by the hard left – and that the violence of recent days is a foretaste of what awaits a dangerously polarised society in the year of elections that is coming. For the right and centre, there is no doubt that behind the student trouble lies the cunning hand of the France Unbowed party (LFI) and its popular presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon. LFI leaders have regularly appeared next to the students – notably in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis whose mayor Bally Bagayoko was criticised for saying that "violence can sometimes be legitimate." Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Bally Bagayoko (left) and presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon (right) have supported the right of the students to protest An internal report prepared for the Paris police department which was leaked to the media analysed the opening of the movement in Seine-Saint-Denis. It concluded that students were being "egged on by far-left elements from students unions… and political groups such as… LFI." It said the tensions "could be part of a flame-kindling strategy… aimed at imposing their ideas ahead of the national elections". In support of its conclusion, the report's writers cited the presence of protesters who are not themselves lycéens , the vagueness of the demands, the flying of Palestinian and Algerian flags, and the use of tactics – like calling for supplementary protests at police-stations - that come from the radical-left playbook. The LFI strongly denies doing anything more than lending its natural support to a movement it regards as legitimate. On Thursday Mélenchon called on students to avoid violence "which only serves our enemies' interests". But his opponents believe that the 75-year-old veteran – who stands a good chance of making it to the second round of the presidential elections in May, probably against the hard-right's Marine Le Pen – knows exactly what he is doing. Polls show he has massive support – some 40% -- among 18-24 year-olds in France, and that this is concentrated in the populous, high-immigration city suburbs where his talk of a "new France" and "creolisation", to reflect France's changing language and population, are highly appreciated. But young people are also the biggest abstainers in French elections, so the strategy – as the elections approach – will be to give constant reminders to this part of the population that the LFI is at their side, and that their vote can count. Whether this will be enough to ensure victory for Mélenchon is another matter.  He must surely take seriously the polls which all show him losing massively in a run-off against Le Pen. If that happens, France will be in very unstable territory - for which the young people's protests of recent days will indeed have been a harbinger. Benefits DOJ Vacancies Legal Careers at DOJ About MT Find Help Contact Us Search Breadcrumb Justice.gov U.S. Attorneys District of Montana Press Releases Billings Man Sentenced To 3 Years In Prison For Unlawfully Possessing a Handgun Press Release Billings man sentenced to 3 years in prison for unlawfully possessing a handgun Friday, October 2, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Montana BILLINGS – A Billings man who was found in his parked car unlawfully carrying a firearm was sentenced Wednesday to three years and one month in prison, followed by three years of supervised release, the U.S. Attorney’s Office announced. William Thomas Fischer, 65, pleaded guilty in May 2026 to unlawfully possessing a firearm. U.S. District Judge Susan P. Watters presided. The government alleged in court documents that Fischer was asleep in a car in the middle of an empty parking lot when police approached to investigate. Startled awake, Fischer immediately began to talk to the officer, who asked Fischer for identification. As Fischer searched the car for documentation, the officer saw the bottom plate of a Glock magazine and ordered him out of the car. After detaining him, officers searched the car and found a handgun, two BB guns, and assorted ammunition. Fischer is a convicted felon and barred from possessing a firearm. The U.S. Attorney’s Office prosecuted the case. The Billings Police Department and ATF conducted the investigation. Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities. Benefits DOJ Vacancies Legal Careers at DOJ About NM Find Help Contact Us Search Breadcrumb Justice.gov U.S. Attorneys District of New Mexico Press Releases U.S. Attorney’s Office Marks Domestic Violence Awareness Month, Highlights Federal Funding For New Mexico Victim Services Press Release U.S. Attorney’s Office Marks Domestic Violence Awareness Month, Highlights Federal Funding for New Mexico Victim Services Friday, October 2, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of New Mexico ALBUQUERQUE – The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of New Mexico joins the Department of Justice, the Office on Violence Against Women and communities across New Mexico in recognizing October as Domestic Violence Awareness Month and reaffirming its commitment to protecting victims, holding offenders accountable and supporting the organizations that serve survivors. “Protecting victims of domestic violence takes coordinated work from law enforcement, prosecutors, advocates and service providers.,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison. “These grants strengthen that work across New Mexico, and our office will continue doing its part to protect victims and pursue offenders under federal law.” As part of that effort, the Department of Justice recently awarded $106,581 to the New Mexico Coalition Against Domestic Violence and $236,484 to the New Mexico Coalition of Sexual Assault Programs, Inc. The two organizations are New Mexico’s designated statewide domestic violence and sexual assault coalitions. “Domestic violence has a devastating impact that reaches far beyond an individual survivor—it affects children, families, communities, and generations,” said MaryEllen Garcia, CEO of New Mexico Coalition Against Domestic Violence. “During Domestic Violence Awareness Month, we honor the courage of survivors while also recognizing the extraordinary work happening every day across New Mexico. The New Mexico Coalition Against Domestic Violence is proud to stand alongside our statewide network of domestic violence providers, whose advocates show up every day with compassion, skill, and an unwavering commitment to survivor safety, dignity, and choice. Ending domestic violence requires all of us—advocates, law enforcement, prosecutors, courts, community partners, and neighbors—working together to build communities where survivors are supported, people who cause harm are held accountable, and everyone has the opportunity to live free from violence.” Domestic Violence Awareness Month provides an opportunity to recognize the work of victim advocates, law enforcement officers, prosecutors, healthcare professionals and community organizations responding to domestic violence throughout New Mexico. It also highlights the role friends, relatives, coworkers and neighbors can play in recognizing abuse and helping victims connect with available resources. The U.S. Attorney’s Office works with federal, Tribal, state and local law enforcement and prosecutors to enforce federal laws applicable to domestic violence, including federal firearms laws intended to keep firearms out of the hands of certain individuals prohibited from possessing them because of domestic violence convictions or qualifying protection orders. The Department of Justice also supports victim services through grant programs administered by the Office on Violence Against Women and the Office for Victims of Crime. OVW identifies the New Mexico Coalition Against Domestic Violence and the New Mexico Coalition of Sexual Assault Programs, Inc. as the state’s designated domestic violence and sexual assault coalitions for fiscal year 2026. Help is available through the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-SAFE (7233) and the StrongHearts Native Helpline at 1-844-7NATIVE (762-8483). Additional resources for victims and survivors are available through the Office on Violence Against Women at justice.gov/ovw. Coleman pleaded guilty to one count of second-degree murder while armed on July 13, 2026, before D.C. Superior Court Judge Danya Dayson. In addition to the 20-year prison sentence, Judge Dayson ordered Coleman to serve five years of supervised release. According to court documents, on November 17, 2023, Coleman attempted to rob Mr. Martinez as Mr. Martinez returned home from a convenience store. Coleman pressed a gun into Mr. Martinez’s head and repeatedly demanded “give it to me.” Mr. Martinez dropped the store bag he was holding but otherwise just stood in place. After the eighth “give it to me,” Coleman pulled the trigger. Mr. Martinez crumpled to the ground, and Coleman walked away. When law enforcement reached Mr. Martinez, his only possession was a single dime. Coleman was arrested on separate charges on February 9, 2024, and has been in custody ever since. Joining the announcement was Interim Chief Jeffery Carroll of the Metropolitan Police Department. In announcing the sentence, U.S. Attorney Pirro and Interim Chief Carroll commended the work of those who investigated the case from the Metropolitan Police Department. They also thanked Assistant U.S. Attorneys Jessica Keefer and William Lawrence, who prosecuted the case. 2025 CF1 008763 Contact USADC.Media@usdoj.gov Updated October 2, 2026 Topics Firearms Offenses Violent Crime Component USAO - District of Columbia Related Content Press Release Virginia Felon Sentenced in D.C. for Possession of Glock Pistol While on Supervised Release Rashim Johnson, 35, a previously convicted felon residing in Warsaw, Virginia, was sentenced today in U.S. District Court in Washington D.C. to 84 months in federal prison in connection with his... Benefits DOJ Vacancies Legal Careers at DOJ About NDNY Find Help Contact Us Search Breadcrumb Justice.gov U.S. Attorneys Northern District of New York Press Releases Oneida County Man Sentenced For Possessing Child Pornography Press Release Oneida County Man Sentenced for Possessing Child Pornography Friday, October 2, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of New York USANYN-MediaInquiry@usa.doj.usa Christopher Pratt, age 40, of Utica, New York, was sentenced on September 10, 2026, to 11 years in federal prison for possessing child pornography. First Assistant United States Attorney John A. Sarcone III and Anthony Patrone, Acting Special Agent in Charge of the Buffalo Field Office of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) made the announcement. As part of his previously entered guilty plea, Pratt admitted that after sustaining a New York State conviction related to child pornography, Pratt possessed numerous images and videos of child pornography on his cell phone, on August 12, 2025. Pratt also admitted that between October of 2023 and January of 2025, he uploaded and distributed child pornography using an online social media application. In addition to the term of imprisonment imposed, United States District Judge Anthony J. Brindisi also imposed a 15-year term of supervised release that will begin after Pratt is released from prison. Pratt was also ordered to pay $27,000 in restitution to the victims of his offense. First Assistant U.S. Attorney Sarcone stated, “I commend our law enforcement partners for their steadfast commitment to protecting children and making sure individuals like the defendant do not remain free in our communities, where they can harm more kids. With the defendant’s disturbing history of child pornography-related offenses, this federal prison term is a just and appropriate punishment.” “This sentence reflects the gravity of Christopher Pratt’s conduct, which included possessing, uploading, and distributing child sexual abuse material after a prior child pornography-related conviction,” said HSI Buffalo Acting Special Agent in Charge Anthony Patrone. “Every file traded online represents a real child victim, and the distribution of this material expands the harm, fuels further exploitation, and undermines the safety of our communities. HSI Syracuse remains unwavering in its commitment to working with our law enforcement partners to pursue those who exploit children and to seek justice for victims.” HSI investigated the case with assistance from the New York State Police and U.S. Customs and Border Protection. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Jessica Carbone and Adrian LaRochelle are prosecuting the case as part of Project Safe Childhood. Project Safe Childhood is a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. Led by the U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the Criminal Division’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS), Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit https://www.justice.gov/psc .
